en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.1 1. Sambodhivagga Sambodhisutta “Monks, there are these nine factors that lead to the attainment of full enlightenment. What nine? (1) Here, monks, a bhikkhu possesses verified confidence in the Buddha thus:

‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses verified confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. (3) He possesses verified confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtue that is both admirable and conducive to concentration. (5) He possesses learning that is both admirable and conducive to concentration. (6) He possesses energy that is both admirable and conducive to concentration. (7) He possesses mindfulness that is both admirable and conducive to concentration. (8) He possesses wisdom that is both admirable and conducive to concentration. (9) He dwells with a mind that has been liberated from the obscurations of the mind, being secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, having entered the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. These, monks, are the nine factors that lead to the attainment of full enlightenment.”
(AN 9.1, PTS AN iv 351) Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you:
‘Friends, what is the proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, bhikkhus, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?”
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One... having heard them from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember them.
“Then listen, bhikkhus, and attend closely; I shall speak,” he said.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects were to ask you thus:
'Friends, what is the proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment?'—being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way:"
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
This, friends, is the first proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, and seeing fear in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training."
Friends, this is the second proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu engages in that kind of talk which is conducive to effacement and favorable to the opening of the mind;
that is to say, talk on fewness of desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtue, and talk on concentration.
Discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation— one obtains such discourse at will,
without difficulty, and without hardship. This, friends,
is the third proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and not relinquishing the burden regarding wholesome states.
This, friends, is the fourth proximate cause for the development of the states conducive to enlightenment.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
“Friends, this is the fifth proximate cause for the development of the qualities conducive to enlightenment.
“It can be expected, monks, of a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate,
that he will be virtuous, dwelling restrained by the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and training himself by undertaking the rules of training.”

“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will engage in discourse that leads to effacement and is conducive to the opening of the mind; that is to say:
discourse on fewness of desires, on contentment, on seclusion, on non-association, on the arousal of energy, on virtue, on concentration, and on wisdom.”
He will be one who gains at will, without difficulty or trouble, talk concerning liberation and talk concerning the knowledge and vision of liberation.

It is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, that he will dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; that he will be steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the duty of cultivating wholesome states.
“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, it is to be expected that he will be wise,
endowed with wisdom regarding the arising and passing away [of phenomena], noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, having established himself in these five qualities, that bhikkhu should develop four further qualities:”

The meditation on the foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thought; the perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit “I am.
For one who perceives impermanence, monks, the perception of non-self becomes established.
One who perceives non-self attains the uprooting of the conceit “I am,” which is Nibbāna in this very life.

Nissaya Sutta (AN 9.2).
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘one endowed with support, one endowed with support.
In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu endowed with support?
“If, bhikkhu, by relying on faith, a bhikkhu abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, that unwholesome state is indeed abandoned by him.”
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu relies on moral shame … [as before] … if,
bhikkhu, a bhikkhu relies on moral dread … [as before] … if,
bhikkhu, a bhikkhu relies on energy … [as before] …
If, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu relies on wisdom to abandon the unwholesome and develop the wholesome, that unwholesome state is indeed abandoned by him.
For that unwholesome state is well-abandoned by that bhikkhu which has been abandoned through seeing with noble wisdom.
Furthermore, bhikkhu, having established himself in these five qualities, that bhikkhu should dwell relying upon four others.
“What four?
Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, endures one thing; having reflected, avoids one thing; having reflected, dispels one thing.
It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu is endowed with support.”
The Second [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.3.
Chapter 1: On Awakening (Sambodhivagga).
The Meghiya Sutta (AN 9.3, PTS AN iv 354).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Cālikā on Mount Cālikā.
Now at that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One’s attendant.

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to enter Jantugāma for alms.”
“Meghiya, you may go at whatever time you think fit.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Meghiya dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Jantugāma for alms.
Having walked for alms in Jantugāma, he returned from his almsround after his meal and approached the bank of the Kimikālā River.
As the Venerable Meghiya was walking and wandering for exercise along the bank of the Kimikālā River, he saw a mango grove that was inspiring and delightful.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
"Truly inspiring is this mango grove, truly delightful; it is indeed sufficient for a son of good family seeking exertion to apply himself to spiritual striving."
“If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would come to this mango grove for the sake of striving.

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, in the morning, having dressed and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Jantu Village for alms.”
Having walked for alms in Jantugāma and returned from my almsround after the meal, I approached the bank of the Kimikālā River.
There, while walking and wandering back and forth along the bank of the Kimikālā River for exercise, I saw a mango grove that was inspiring and delightful.
Upon seeing it, this thought occurred to me:
‘This mango grove is indeed serene and delightful.
It is surely sufficient for a son of good family who seeks to strive in the practice of meditation.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would come to this mango grove to strive in meditation.’
“If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would go to that mango grove for the sake of striving.
“Wait a moment, Meghiya, until some other monk arrives; it is not right for you to go alone.
A second time, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for the Blessed One there is nothing further to be done, and there is no addition to what has been accomplished.
But for me, venerable sir, there is still more to be done, and there is an addition to what has been accomplished.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would go to that mango grove for the sake of striving.”
“Wait a moment, Meghiya; stay alone for as long as it takes until some other monk arrives.
For a third time, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, there is nothing further for the Blessed One to do; there is nothing more to be added to what has been done.”
“But, Bhante, there is still more for me to do, and there is further work to be done.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would go to that mango grove to practice striving.
“Meghiya, when one speaks of ‘striving,’ what could we possibly say?”
“Meghiya, you may go at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then the Venerable Meghiya rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, he went to that mango grove.
Having arrived and entered deep into that mango grove, he went to a certain spot...
He sat at the foot of a tree for his midday rest.
Then, as the Venerable Meghiya was dwelling in that mango grove, for the most part three kinds of evil, unwholesome thoughts occurred to him:
namely, thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Meghiya:
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
For we have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith.”
"Moreover, he is obsessed with these three kinds of evil, unwholesome thoughts:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was dwelling in that mango grove, for the most part three kinds of unwholesome, unskillful thoughts occurred to me:
namely, sensual thought, ill will thought, and harmfulness thought.
Then, Bhante, this occurred to me:”
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
For although we have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, we are nevertheless still beset by these three kinds of evil, unwholesome thoughts.’
“...by thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
“Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, five things lead to its maturation.
What are the five?
"Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
For one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, Meghiya, this is the first quality that leads to its maturation.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, and seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the rules of training."
Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, this is the second thing that leads to its maturation.
Furthermore, Meghiya, there is this talk that is conducive to effacement and favorable to the opening of the mind; that is to say:
talk on fewness of desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtue, and talk on concentration.
Discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation— one obtains such talk as one desires,
without difficulty and without hardship. Meghiya,
for one whose mental liberation is not yet matured, this is the third quality that leads to its maturation.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish the burden regarding wholesome states.
Meghiya, this is the fourth quality that leads to the ripening of the mind’s liberation when it is not yet ripened.
Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is unripened, this is the fifth quality that leads to its ripening.
For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate, Meghiya, it is to be expected that he will be virtuous...
[and so on] ...and will train himself by undertaking the training rules.

For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has good companions and good associates, it is to be expected that he will obtain at will, without difficulty or trouble, whatever talk is conducive to effacement and helpful for opening the mind—namely, talk on fewness of desires... up to ... talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation.

For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has a good companion, who has a good associate, it is to be expected that he will dwell with energy aroused, [and so on]... not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states.

For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has a good companion, who has a good associate, it is to be expected that he will become wise, [and so on]... leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
Furthermore, Meghiya, having established himself in these five qualities, a bhikkhu should further develop four other qualities:

"The meditation on the foul should be developed for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thoughts; and the perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit 'I am.
For one who perceives impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established.
One who perceives non-self attains the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' and realizes Nibbāna in this very life."
The Third [Sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.4.
1. The Chapter on Enlightenment (Sambodhivagga).
The Discourse to Nandaka (AN 9.4).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Nandaka was in the assembly hall instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he stood outside the door, waiting for the conclusion of the talk.
Then, knowing the talk had concluded, the Blessed One cleared his throat and knocked on the bolt.
Those bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the assembly hall, sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Nandaka:
“Nandaka, this exposition of the Dhamma that appeared to you for the bhikkhus is indeed long.
My back is aching as I have been standing outside the gateway waiting for the conclusion of the discourse.
When this was said, the Venerable Nandaka, appearing somewhat abashed, said this to the Blessed One:
“But we did not know, Bhante, that the Blessed One was standing outside the gatehouse.
For if we had known, Bhante, that the Blessed One was standing outside the gatehouse, we would not have spoken even this much.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the Venerable Nandaka appeared embarrassed, said to the Venerable Nandaka:
“Excellent, excellent, Nandaka!
This is indeed worthy of you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, that you should sit together in discourse on the Dhamma.
When you have assembled, Nandaka, two things are to be done:”
Either a discourse on the Dhamma or noble silence.
Now, Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith but not possessed of virtue;
thus he is incomplete in that respect.
Therefore, that factor should be fulfilled by thinking:
"How may I be endowed with faith and possessed of virtue?
But when, Nandaka, a bhikkhu is both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue, he is thus complete in that factor.
"Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and virtuous, yet he is not an attainer of internal mental concentration.
In this way, he is incomplete in that factor.
Therefore, that factor should be fulfilled by him: [as follows...]"
‘But what if I were to be endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, and a gainer of internal mental concentration?
Nandaka, when a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, and a gainer of internal mental concentration, he is thus fulfilled in that factor.
However, Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith, possessed of virtue, and a gainer of internal mental concentration, yet not be a gainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
In this way, he is incomplete in that respect.
Nandaka, it is just as if there were a four-legged creature,
one of whose legs was deficient and defective.
In this way, he would be incomplete in that respect.
In the same way, Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith, virtuous, and a possessor of internal mental concentration, yet not a possessor of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
In this way, he is incomplete in that respect.
Therefore, that factor should be fulfilled by him:
"How may I be endowed with faith and virtuous, and be a gainer of internal mental concentration and a gainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena?

But when, Nandaka, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith and virtuous, and is a gainer of internal mental concentration and a gainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena, then he is complete in that factor.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Nandaka addressed the bhikkhus:
“Now, friend, after the Blessed One had proclaimed the entirely complete and pure holy life in four statements, he rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
‘Nandaka, a bhikkhu may have faith but not be virtuous;
thus he is incomplete in that respect.’”
Therefore, that factor must be fulfilled by him:
‘How can I be both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue?
But when, Nandaka, a bhikkhu is both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue, he is thus complete in that factor.
“Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and virtuous, yet he is not an attainer of internal mental concentration...
[or] he may be an attainer of internal mental concentration, yet he is not an attainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena;
thus, he is incomplete in that respect.”
"Just as if, Nandaka, there were a four-footed creature, and one of its feet were deficient and defective;
thus it would be incomplete in that limb.
Even so, Nandaka, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and virtuous, and he may be a possessor of internal mental concentration, yet he is not a possessor of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena."
In this way, he is incomplete in that factor;
therefore, that factor must be fulfilled [with the thought]:
"How may I be endowed with faith and virtuous conduct, and be a possessor of internal mental concentration, and a possessor of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena?"
But when, Nandaka, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith and virtuous, and is a gainer of internal mental concentration and a gainer of higher wisdom and insight into phenomena,
then he is complete in that respect.
"Friends, there are these five benefits in listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and in discussing the Dhamma at the proper time."
Which five?

Here, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, proclaiming the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
In whatever way, friends, the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle... [and so on].
He proclaims the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
in such a way, he becomes dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by the Teacher.
This, friends, is the first benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life in its full perfection and purity.
In whatever way, friends, the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—good in the beginning... [and so forth].
He proclaims the holy life in such a way that he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma within that teaching.
This, friends, is the second benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and engaging in discussion on the Dhamma at the proper time.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and beautiful in the end—with the right meaning and phrasing; he proclaims the holy life, entirely complete and pure.

"In whatever way, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beginning well... [and so on] ...and reveals the holy life—in that very way he penetrates with wisdom and sees the profound meaning of that Dhamma.
This, friends, is the third benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beginning well... [and so on] ...and reveals the holy life."

In whatever way, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—beginning well... [and so on] ...and reveals the holy life, in that same way his fellow practitioners hold him in higher esteem, thinking:
"Surely this venerable one has attained it, or is attaining it.
This, friends, is the fourth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and engaging in discussion on the Dhamma at the proper time.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.

In whatever way, friends, that bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing—he reveals the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
He proclaims it; and there, those monks who are trainees (*śaikṣa*), whose minds have not yet reached fulfillment, and who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage,
upon hearing that Dharma, arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the reaching of the unreached,
and for the realization of the unrealized.

But those bhikkhus there who are arahants— whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted,
and who are liberated through right gnosis— having heard that Dhamma, dwell devoted solely to a pleasant abiding here and now. This, friends,
is the fifth benefit of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and engaging in discussion on the Dhamma at the proper time.
“Friends, these are the five benefits of listening to the Dhamma at the proper time and discussing the Dhamma at the proper time.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.5

1. Sambodhivagga Balasutta (AN 9.5, PTS AN iv 363) “Monks, there are these five powers. What five? The power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. These, monks, are the five powers.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four powers.
What are the four?
The power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of blamelessness, and the power of gathering.”
And what, monks, is the power of wisdom?
Those states which are wholesome and reckoned as wholesome; those states which are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome; those states which are blameworthy and reckoned as blameworthy;
those states which are blameless and reckoned as blameless; those states which are dark and reckoned as dark.

Those phenomena which are bright and reckoned as bright; those phenomena which are to be cultivated and reckoned as to be cultivated; those phenomena which are not to be cultivated and reckoned as not to be cultivated;

those phenomena which are not sufficient for a noble one and reckoned as not sufficient for a noble one; and those phenomena which are sufficient for a noble one and reckoned as sufficient for a noble one—all these phenomena have been clearly seen and thoroughly mastered by him through wisdom.
This, monks, is called the power of wisdom.
And what, monks, is the power of energy?
Those states that are unwholesome, reckoned as unwholesome; those states that are blameworthy, reckoned as blameworthy; those states that are dark...

He generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of those states reckoned as dark, which are reckoned as not to be cultivated; and of those states reckoned as unworthy of an Ariyan, which are reckoned as unworthy of an Ariyan.
He generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the cultivation of those states reckoned as wholesome, which are reckoned as wholesome;
those states reckoned as blameless, which are reckoned as blameless; and those states reckoned as bright.
Those states reckoned as bright which are to be cultivated, and those states reckoned as noble which are worthy of the noble ones—
by way of obtaining these states, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses energy,
uplifts the mind, and strives. This, monks, is called the power of energy.
And what, monks, is the power of blamelessness?
Here, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, and endowed with blameless mental action.
This, monks, is called the power of blamelessness.
And what, monks, is the power of attraction?
There are these four bases of attraction, monks:
generosity, amiable speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
“Monks, this is the foremost of gifts: the gift of the Dhamma.
Monks, this is the foremost of kindly words: to teach the Dhamma again and again to one who is in need and who lends an ear.
Monks, this is the foremost of beneficial conducts: to encourage one lacking faith toward the perfection of faith.”
He encourages, settles, and establishes the immoral in the perfection of virtue; he encourages, settles, and establishes the stingy in the perfection of generosity;
he encourages, settles, and establishes the unwise in the perfection of wisdom.

This, monks, is the foremost among equalities: namely, a stream-enterer is equal to a stream-enterer, a once-returner is equal to a once-returner, a non-returner is equal to a non-returner, and an arahant is equal to an arahant.
This, monks, is called the power of gathering.
These, monks, are the four powers.
Possessed of these four powers, monks, the noble disciple has transcended five fears.
Which five?
Fear for one’s livelihood, fear of ill-repute, fear of timidity before assemblies, fear of death, and fear of a miserable rebirth.
That noble disciple, bhikkhus, reflects thus:
“I am not afraid of the fear of livelihood.
Why should I be afraid of the fear of livelihood?
For I possess four powers.”
The power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of blamelessness, and the power of gathering [the community].
One who is lacking in wisdom might fear for his livelihood;
one who is lazy might fear for his livelihood.
One who engages in blameworthy bodily, verbal, and mental actions would fear for their livelihood;
one who does not cultivate [wholesome qualities] would fear for their livelihood.
But I do not fear ill repute … [and so on].
I do not fear the fear of being censured by the assembly …pe… I do not fear the fear of death …pe… I do not fear the fear of an unhappy rebirth.
Why should I fear the danger of an unhappy rebirth?
I possess four powers:
the power of wisdom, the power of energy, the power of blamelessness, and the power of gathering [the community].
One who is lacking wisdom should fear the danger of an unhappy destination.
One who is lazy should fear the danger of an unhappy destination.
One whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions are blameworthy should fear the danger of an unhappy destination.
“One who lacks a supportive friend would fear the danger of an unhappy destination.
“Monks, an noble disciple endowed with these four powers has completely transcended these five fears.
Thus was the fifth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.6 1. Sambodhivagga Sevanāsutta – The Discourse on Cultivation “Monks, there are these nine persons found existing in the world. What nine?

The person who is a murderer, the person who is a thief, the person who is a libertine, the person who is a liar, the person who is a slanderer, the person who is a harsh speaker, the person who is a frivolous talker, the person who is covetous, and the person who holds wrong view. These, monks, are the nine persons found existing in the world. These nine persons, monks, when cultivated, frequented, and served, lead to decline, not to distinction. There are, monks, these other nine persons found existing in the world. What nine? The person who abstains from killing, the person who abstains from stealing, the person who abstains from sexual misconduct, the person who abstains from false speech, the person who abstains from divisive speech, the person who abstains from harsh speech, the person who abstains from frivolous talk, the person who is uncovetous, and the person who holds right view. These, monks, are the nine persons found existing in the world. These nine persons, monks, when cultivated, frequented, and served, lead to distinction, not to decline.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “… [as before] …” The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, a person is also to be understood in two ways:”
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Likewise, friends, a robe should be understood as being of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
"Friends, almsfood too should be understood as twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
Lodgings too, friends, should be understood as twofold."
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
A village or town, friend, should also be understood as twofold:
that which should be frequented and that which should not be frequented.
"A region, friend, should also be understood in two ways:
as one to be cultivated and one not to be cultivated.
A person, friend, should also be understood in two ways—"
‘There is one who should be cultivated and one who should not be cultivated’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In that regard, suppose one should know of a person:
‘When I associate with this person, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline;
furthermore, those requisites of life that must be procured by one gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained with difficulty;
and that goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which I went forth from the home life into homelessness does not reach fulfillment through development.’
‘He is going,’ then, friends, that person should depart from that other person at any time— whether by night or by day—
even without informing him, and should not follow after him.
In this regard, one should know of that person:
‘When I associate with this person, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline;
while those requisites of life that must be procured by one gone forth— robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— are obtained without difficulty,
yet that goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which I went forth from the home life into homelessness does not reach fulfillment through development.’
‘He is going,’ then, friends, that person should depart from that other person even without informing him and should not follow after him.
In this regard, one should know of a person:
‘When I associate with this person, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.’”
‘Those requisites of life that must be procured by one who has gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for use in sickness—are obtained with difficulty by me;

and as for the goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which I went forth from the home life into homelessness, that goal of the ascetic life does not reach fulfillment through my development. In such a case, friends, that person should follow that other person even against their will; they should not depart.
In this regard, if one should know of a person:
‘By associating with this person, unwholesome states diminish in me and wholesome states increase;
furthermore, those requisites of life that must be procured by one gone forth—robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—are obtained without difficulty;
and as for the goal of the ascetic life for the sake of which I went forth from the home life into homelessness, that goal of asceticism reaches full development in me.’
‘He is going,’ friend; therefore, that person should follow that other person for as long as life lasts and not depart, even if being sent away.
‘A person, friend, is to be understood in two ways:
one who is to be associated with and one who is not to be associated with.’”
Thus, that which was said—
"Friends, robes too should be understood in two ways:
those to be used and those not to be used"— was said with reference to this.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, if one should know of a robe:
"While I am using this robe, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a robe should not be used.
In this regard, whatever robe one should know of thus:
"While using this robe of mine, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase"—such a robe should be used.
"Furthermore, friends, a robe should be understood in two ways:..."
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
it was with reference to this that it was said.
‘Almsfood, friend, should also be understood as twofold:’
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, one should know of almsfood: [that it should be cultivated or not].
‘If, while consuming this almsfood, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish,’ such almsfood should not be consumed.
But in that case, one should know of the almsfood:
‘If, while consuming this almsfood, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase,’ such almsfood should be consumed.
‘Almsfood too, friends, should be understood to be twofold:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
“‘Friends, dwellings also should be understood as twofold:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
So it was said. With reference to what was this said?”
In that regard, if one should know of a lodging:
"When I frequent this lodging, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a lodging should not be frequented.
In that regard, if one should know of a lodging:
‘When I use this lodging, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase’—such a lodging should be used.
“Friends, a lodging should also be understood as twofold:
that which is to be used and that which is not to be used.”

Thus, that which was said— "Friends, a village or town is to be understood as twofold: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated"— it is in reference to this that it was said.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, if one should know of a village or town:
"By frequenting this village or town, unwholesome states increase in me and wholesome states decline," then such a village or town should not be frequented.
In that regard, if one should know of a village or town:
"When I associate with this village or town, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase," such a village or town should be frequented.
"Friends, a village or town should also be understood as being of two kinds."
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘A region, friend, should also be understood as twofold:’
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, one should know of a certain region:
‘While I am frequenting this region, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline’—such a region should not be frequented.
However, regarding a region where one should know:
‘While I am frequenting this region, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase’—such a region should be frequented.
“‘A country district, friend, should also be understood in two ways:
as one to be cultivated and as one not to be cultivated.
It was with reference to this that it was said.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.7 1.
Sambodhivagga (The Chapter on Full Enlightenment)
Sutavāsutta (AN 9.7).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
Then the wanderer Suta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Suta said this to the Blessed One:
"Bhante, on one occasion I was staying right here in Rājagaha, at Giribbaja."
In this regard, venerable sir, I have heard and received it directly from the Blessed One’s presence:

“Bhikkhus, that learned bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing five things.
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of [the other four].”
“A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, reckoned as theft; he is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse; he is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie;
he is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding, just as he did formerly when he was a householder.”
“Venerable sir, have I heard this well from the Blessed One, grasped it well, attended to it well, and retained it well?
“Indeed, Sutavā, you have heard this well from me, grasped it well, attended to it well, and retained it well.
Both formerly, Sutavā, and now, I say this:”

‘That bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing nine points:
an arahant bhikkhu with taints destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life;
an arahant bhikkhu with taints destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, in the form of theft; an arahant bhikkhu with taints destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse.’
A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie;
a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding them, as he did formerly when he was a householder;

a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of falling into a wrong course through desire, incapable of falling into a wrong course through hatred, and incapable of falling into a wrong course through delusion.
“...he is incapable of going on a path out of fear.
Both formerly, Sutavā, and now as well, I say this:

“That bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—he is incapable of transgressing these nine points.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.8 1.
Sambodhivagga (The Chapter on Enlightenment)
The Sajjha Sutta (AN 9.8).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then the wanderer Sajjha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Sajjha said this to the Blessed One:
"On one occasion, venerable sir, the Blessed One was staying right here in Rājagaha, at Giribbaja."
In this regard, venerable sir, I have heard and received it directly from the Blessed One’s presence:

“Sajjha, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge, is incapable of transgressing five things.
An arahant bhikkhu with taints destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life; an arahant bhikkhu with taints destroyed is incapable of...”
‘An arahant bhikkhu is incapable of taking what is not given, which is reckoned as theft; an arahant bhikkhu is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse;
an arahant bhikkhu is incapable of speaking a deliberate lie; an arahant bhikkhu is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by storing them up, just as he did formerly when he was a householder.’”
“Venerable sir, has this been well heard, well grasped, well attended to, and well remembered by me?
“Indeed, Sajjha, it has been well heard, well grasped, well attended to, and well remembered by you.
Both formerly, Sajjha, and now, I speak thus:”

‘That monk who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis—he is incapable of transgressing nine points:
an arahant monk with taints destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life...
[and so on] ...an arahant monk with taints destroyed is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures by means of hoarding, as he did formerly when he was a householder; he is incapable.’
‘A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of renouncing the Buddha; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of renouncing the Dhamma;
a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of renouncing the Saṅgha; a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of renouncing the training.
Both formerly, Sajjha, and now as well, I say this:

“Bhikkhus, that bhikkhu who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained his own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who is liberated through right gnosis—is incapable of transgressing these nine points.
The eighth.

1. Sambodhivagga Puggalasutta (AN 9.9, PTS AN iv 372) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, yet he does not encourage others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, yet he encourages others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, monks, is one a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, nor does he encourage others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, monks, is one a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, and he encourages others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these nine persons are found existing in the world.
Which nine?
The arahant, one practicing for arahantship; the non-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the once-returner, [and so forth].”
"One practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, a stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry,
and an ordinary person—
these, monks, are the nine persons existing and found in the world."
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.10 1.
Sambodhivagga (The Chapter on Enlightenment)
Āhuneyyasutta: “Monks,
these nine persons are worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
Which nine? The arahant; one practicing for arahantship; the non-returner; one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; the once-returner;
one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the stream-enterer; and one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
“...the one practicing the way, and the one who has reached the stage of change-of-lineage—these, monks, are the nine persons worthy of gifts ... the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.

Sambodhi and Nissaya.
Meghiya, Nandaka, and Bala;

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.11 2.
Sīhanādavagga Sīhanādasutta (The Lion’s Roar)
(AN 9.11, PTS AN iv 373) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, my rains residence at Sāvatthī is completed.
Venerable sir, I wish to set out on a journey through the countryside.
“Sāriputta, you may go at whatever time you deem appropriate.”
Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after the Venerable Sāriputta had left, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has set out on his alms round after having insulted me and not apologizing."
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address Sāriputta in my name, saying:
‘Friend Sāriputta, the Teacher calls you.’”
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the Venerable Sāriputta and said to him:
“Friend Sāriputta, the Teacher calls you.
“Very well, friend,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to that bhikkhu.
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Ānanda were walking about in the monastery carrying keys, saying:
"Come forth, venerable sirs! Come forth, venerable sirs!
Now the Venerable Sāriputta will roar his lion’s roar in the presence of the Blessed One."

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Sāriputta, here a certain fellow celibate has fallen into a state of reproach, saying:
‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta, having assailed me, set out on his alms-round without apologizing.’”

“Venerable sir, it would surely be one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established who, having offended against some fellow practitioner here and failing to relinquish that offense,
would set out on a journey. Venerable sir, just as they place both the pure and the impure upon the earth—
placing excrement, urine, spittle, pus, and blood there— ”
They even discard blood, yet the earth does not feel repelled, ashamed, or disgusted by it.
In the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like the earth—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

Venerable sir, if anyone were not established in mindfulness directed to the body regarding their own person, they might, having offended against some fellow practitioner here, set out on a journey without making amends for that offense.
Just as, venerable sir, people wash both the clean and the unclean in water— washing even what consists of feces,
urine, spittle, pus, and blood— and yet the water is not distressed,
ashamed, or disgusted by it;
In this very way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like water—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

Venerable sir, if one were not established in mindfulness directed to the body regarding the body, he might, having offended against some fellow practitioner here, set out on his journey without making amends.
Just as fire, venerable sir, burns both the pure and the impure, including even excrement and urine.
… it burns even what has reached the saliva, even what has reached the phlegm, even what has reached the blood, yet that fire is not distressed,
ashamed, or disgusted by it; in the same way, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like fire— vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

"Venerable sir, it is possible that one whose mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might, having offended against some fellow practitioner here, set out on a journey without making amends. Venerable sir,
just as the wind blows upon what is pure and what is impure— blowing upon excrement, urine, spittle, pus, and blood— the wind is not repelled by that."
"Or feels aversion, or feels disgust;
even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like the wind—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

Indeed, Bhante, one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might, having offended against some fellow practitioner here, set out on a journey without relinquishing that offense."
"Venerable sir, just as a dust-remover wipes away both the clean and the unclean—
it wipes away what has become excrement, urine, spittle, pus, or blood—
and yet the dust-remover is not thereby distressed, ashamed, or disgusted;"
"In this very way, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like a dust-remover—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
Bhante, if one were not established in mindfulness directed to the body regarding the body, they might, having offended some fellow practitioner here, set out on a journey without apologizing.

Just as a young Caṇḍāla boy or girl, carrying a basket and clad in rags, enters a village or town while maintaining a humble mind; even so, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like a dust-remover—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will."
"In this very way, Bhante, I dwell with a mind like that of a young Caṇḍāla boy or a young Caṇḍāla girl—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

Indeed, Bhante, one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might, having provoked some fellow celibate practitioner here and not relinquishing that provocation, set out on a journey."

"Venerable sir, just as a bull with its horns cut off—gentle, well-tamed, and well-trained—wanders from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads without harming anything with its feet or its horns;
even so, venerable sir, I dwell with a mind like that of a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will."

"Venerable sir, surely one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might, having offended against some fellow practitioner here and not making amends for it, set out on a journey.

Just as, venerable sir, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of ornaments, and having washed their heads—would be repelled, ashamed, and disgusted by a snake’s carcass, a dog’s carcass, or a human carcass hanging from their neck;
even so, venerable sir, am I repelled, ashamed, and disgusted by this putrid body."

"Venerable sir, it would surely be the case that one in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might set out on tour here after having offended against some fellow celibate practitioner and not relinquishing that offense.
Just as if, venerable sir, a man were carrying a cracked and perforated oil-skin, leaking and dripping;
even so, venerable sir, do I carry this body, cracked and perforated, leaking and dripping."

“Venerable sir, surely he in whose body mindfulness directed to the body has not been established might here, having provoked some fellow practitioner of the holy life and not relinquishing that provocation, set out on his wanderings.
Then that bhikkhu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said this to the Blessed One:

“A transgression has overcome me, venerable sir; it was like that of a fool, like that of a deluded man, like that of an unskillful person, in that I falsely, vainly, and untruthfully misrepresented the Venerable Sāriputta.”
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my transgression as a transgression for the sake of future restraint.
“Indeed, monk, you have committed a transgression—just as one who is foolish, deluded, and unskilled—who falsely, vainly, and falsely misrepresented Sāriputta with what is untrue.
But since you, monk, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.”

“Bhikkhu, this is growth in the discipline of the Noble One: when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Forgive this misguided man, Sāriputta, before his head splits into seven pieces right there.”
“I forgive that venerable one, Bhante, if that venerable one says to me:
‘And may that venerable one forgive me.
First.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.12 2. Sīhanādavagga Saupādisesasutta The Discourse on One with a Remnant Remaining “Monks, there is the case where a monk is one with a remnant remaining. He dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of devas.

There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of higher devas. There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of still higher devas. There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of even higher devas. There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of yet higher devas. There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of the highest devas. There he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. “Just as when a man throws a ball of string into the air, it rolls along unwinding until it comes to rest right there; in the same way, monks, a monk who is one with a remnant remaining dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a certain company of devas... [as above] ...there he dwells having attained the deliverance of mind that is beautiful, radiant, and has reached the ultimate perfection of mental cultivation. “This, monks, is called a monk who is one with a remnant remaining.”
(AN 9.12, PTS AN iv 378) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, in the morning,
the Venerable Sāriputta dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī;
what if I were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?"
Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the park of those wanderers of other sects; having approached, he exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side.
Now at that time, while those wanderers of other sects were seated together in assembly, this discussion arose among them:

“Friends, whoever dies with a residue remaining is entirely not freed from hell, not freed from the animal realm, not freed from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and not freed from states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta neither rejoiced in nor rejected the statement of those wanderers of other sects.
Without rejoicing and without rejecting it, he rose from his seat and departed.
“I shall understand the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī, the Venerable Sāriputta returned from his almsround after his meal and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then, Bhante, this thought occurred to me:”
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī;
what if I were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?
Then, venerable sir, I went to the park of the wanderers of other sects, and having arrived, I exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, I sat down to one side.
Now at that time, while those wanderers of other sects were sitting together in assembly, this discussion arose among them:

“Friends, whoever dies with a residue remaining, all such persons are not freed from hell, not freed from the animal realm, not freed from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and not freed from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.”
Then, venerable sir, I neither rejoiced in nor rejected the speech of those wanderers of other sects.
Without rejoicing and without rejecting it, I rose from my seat and departed, thinking:
"I shall learn the meaning of this speech in the presence of the Blessed One."

“Sāriputta, what ignorant and incompetent wanderers of other sects could possibly know one who has a residue remaining as ‘having a residue remaining,’ or one who has no residue remaining as ‘having no residue remaining’?

Sāriputta, these nine persons, when passing away with a residue remaining, are freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of afflicted spirits, and freed from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms. Which nine? [The text continues with the description of these nine individuals.]”
"Here, Sāriputta, a certain person fulfills his duties regarding virtue, fulfills his duties regarding concentration, and practices wisdom to a moderate degree.
Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final Nibbāna in the interval.

This, Sāriputta, is the first person who, when passing away while still possessing a residue of clinging, is liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, liberated from the sphere of ghosts, and liberated from states of deprivation, ill destiny, and perdition."
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person is one who fulfills virtuous conduct, fulfills concentration, and practices wisdom to a moderate degree.
Through the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains nibbāna upon landing...
[or] one who attains nibbāna without exertion... [and so forth].
He attains final nibbāna with exertion … he becomes one who goes upstream,

bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm. This, Sāriputta, is the fifth person who, at the time of death, while still possessing a residue of clinging, is liberated from hell, liberated from the animal realm, liberated from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and liberated from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person is one who fulfills the moral precepts, but is only partial in concentration and partial in wisdom.
With the total destruction of three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hate, and delusion, he becomes a once-returner; returning only once more to this world, he makes an end of suffering.

This, Sāriputta, is the sixth person who, when passing away with a residue remaining, is freed from hell... [and so on] ...freed from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person fulfills his conduct in the precepts, but practices concentration only to a moderate degree, and practices wisdom only to a moderate degree.
With the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes a "single-seed" (ekabījī); having produced only one more human existence, he makes an end of suffering.

This, Sāriputta, is the seventh person who, when passing away with a residue remaining, is liberated from hell... [and so on] ...liberated from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person fulfills virtuous conduct, but practices concentration only to a moderate degree, and practices wisdom only to a moderate degree.
With the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes a "family-to-family" attainer; having wandered and transmigrated among two or three families, he makes an end of suffering.

This, Sāriputta, is the eighth person who, when passing away with a residue remaining, is liberated from hell... [and so on] ...is liberated from the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here a certain person fulfills virtuous conduct, but practices concentration only to a moderate degree, and practices wisdom only to a moderate degree.

With the total destruction of three fetters, he becomes one who returns at most seven times; having wandered and transmigrated among devas and humans for seven more existences at most, he makes an end of suffering.

This, Sāriputta, is the ninth person who, when passing away with a residue remaining, is freed from hell, freed from the animal realm, freed from the sphere of hungry ghosts, and freed from states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition.

And what, Sāriputta, are these foolish and incompetent wanderers of other sects, that they would know one with a residue remaining as "with a residue remaining," or know one without a residue remaining as "without a residue remaining"?

"These nine persons, Sāriputta, when passing away with a residue remaining, are freed from hell, freed from the animal womb, freed from the realm of hungry ghosts, and freed from states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition.
Yet, Sāriputta, this exposition of the Dhamma did not occur to the minds of the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen.
For what reason?"
“Having heard this discourse on the Dhamma, they brought about negligence.
“Moreover, Sāriputta, this discourse on the Dhamma was spoken by me with a specific purpose in mind.
This is the second [sutta].

(AN 9.13, PTS AN iv 382) Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, is it for this purpose that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that whatever karma is to be experienced in the present life, may that karma become karma to be experienced in a future life?
“No indeed, friend.

“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for this purpose that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that whatever karma is to be experienced in a future life, may that karma become karma to be experienced in the present life?”
“No, friend.
“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for this purpose that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that ‘may my karma which is to be experienced as pleasant become karma to be experienced as painful’?
“No, friend.”

“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose of thinking, ‘May this karma that is to be experienced as painful become for me karma to be experienced as pleasant,’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?
“No indeed, friend.

“Then, friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose of thinking, ‘May this karma that is to be experienced upon ripening become for me karma to be experienced without ripening,’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?”
“No, friend.

“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for this purpose that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that ‘whatever karma is to be experienced when not yet ripened, may that karma become for me to be experienced when ripened’?
“No, friend.”
“Friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose, ‘May this karma of mine that is to be experienced as much become karma to be experienced as little,’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?
“No, friend.
“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose, ‘May this karma of mine that is to be experienced as little become karma to be experienced as much,’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?”
“No, friend.

“But what then, friend Sāriputta—is it for the purpose of thinking, ‘May this kamma that is to be experienced become kamma not to be experienced by me,’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?
“No, friend.”
“But, friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose that ‘whatever karma is not to be experienced, may that karma become experienceable by me’ that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?
“No indeed, friend.
“Then, friend Sāriputta, is it for the purpose that ‘whatever karma is to be experienced in this very life, may that karma become experienceable in a future life’?”
‘...let it be so; for this purpose the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being asked thus, you say, ‘Not so, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, that action which is to be experienced in a future life—can that action be made to be experienced in the present life?’”
‘May it be so,’ for the sake of this the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being thus asked, you say, ‘Not so, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is that action which is to be experienced as pleasant instead for you an action to be experienced as painful?’
‘May it be so’—for this purpose the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being asked thus, you say, ‘No indeed, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is that action which is to be experienced as painful for you to be experienced as pleasant?’”
‘May it be so’—for this purpose the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being asked thus, you say, ‘Not so, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is that karma which is to be experienced when fully ripened to be experienced by me when not yet ripened?’
‘May it be so’—for the sake of this, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being asked thus, you say: ‘Not so, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is that kamma which was to be experienced when unripe now to be experienced by me when ripe?’
‘Let it be so’—for this purpose the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
Being asked thus, you say, ‘Certainly not, friend.
‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is that karma which is to be experienced as much [suffering] to be experienced by me as little?’”
‘...that “let it be so,” for the sake of this the holy life is lived under the Blessed One’— when asked thus,
you say, ‘No indeed,
friend. ‘But then, friend Sāriputta, is it that by saying, “Let my karma which is to be experienced as little become karma to be experienced as much,”’” [you mean this?]

‘Is it for this purpose, friend, that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that whatever karma is to be experienced shall instead become karma not to be experienced?’—being asked thus, you replied, ‘No indeed, friend.

‘Then, friend Sāriputta, is it for this purpose that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One—that whatever karma is to be experienced shall instead become karma not to be experienced?’—being asked thus, you replied, ‘No indeed, friend.’”

“But, friend Sāriputta, when you were asked: ‘Is it for the purpose that whatever karma is not to be felt may instead become karma to be felt by me that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?’—being thus questioned, you replied: ‘Certainly not, friend.
Then for what purpose, friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One?”

“Friend, it is for the sake of knowing, seeing, attaining, realizing, and fully penetrating that which has not been known, seen, attained, realized, and fully penetrated, that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.

But what, friend, is that which has not been known, seen, attained, realized, and fully penetrated, for the sake of knowing, seeing, attaining, realizing, and fully penetrating which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One?”
"Friends, 'This is suffering'—this has not been known by him, seen, attained, realized, and fully understood.
It is for the sake of knowing, seeing, attaining, realizing, and fully understanding this that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
'This is the origin of suffering,' friends... [as before] ... 'This is the cessation of suffering,' friends... [as before]"
"‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’—this, friend, has not been known, seen, attained, realized, and fully understood by him.
It is for the sake of knowing, seeing, attaining, realizing, and fully understanding this that the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.
This, friend, is what has not been known, seen, attained, realized, and fully understood by him."
“The holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of vision, for the sake of attainment, for the sake of realization, and for the sake of penetration.
The third.

2. Sīhanādavagga Samiddhisutta (AN 9.14, PTS AN iv 385)
Then the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Venerable Sāriputta;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Samiddhi was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to him:
“Samiddhi, with what as their object do a person’s intentions and thoughts arise?
“With name-and-form as their object, venerable sir.
“But where, Samiddhi, do they reach diversity?”
“Regarding the elements, venerable sir.
“But what, Samiddhi, is their origin?
“Contact is their origin, venerable sir.”
“But what, Samiddhi, do they converge upon?
“They converge upon feeling, Bhante.
“But what, Samiddhi, are they headed by?”
“Concentration is foremost, venerable sir.
“But what, Samiddhi, is their governing principle?
“Mindfulness is the governing principle, venerable sir.”
“But what, Samiddhi, is their culmination?
“Wisdom, Bhante.
“But what, Samiddhi, is their core?”
“Liberation is their essence, Bhante.
“But in what, Samiddhi, are they grounded?
“The deathless is their ground, Bhante.”
“When you were asked, ‘Samiddhi, with what as their object do a person’s intentions and thoughts arise? you replied, ‘Venerable sir, with name-and-form as their object.
When you were asked, ‘But Samiddhi, where do they find their diversity? you replied, ‘Venerable sir, in the elements.
When you were asked, ‘But Samiddhi, what is their origin? you replied, ‘Venerable sir, contact is their origin.’”
“When you were asked, ‘But, Samiddhi, what do they converge upon? you replied, ‘They converge upon feeling, venerable sir.
When you were asked, ‘But, Samiddhi, what is their foremost? you replied, ‘Concentration is their foremost, venerable sir.
When you were asked, ‘But, Samiddhi, what is their governing principle? you replied, ‘Mindfulness is their governing principle, venerable sir.’”
“Being asked, ‘But what, Samiddhi, is their excellence? you replied, ‘Wisdom, Bhante.
Being asked, ‘But what, Samiddhi, is their essence? you replied, ‘Liberation, Bhante.
Being asked, ‘But what, Samiddhi, is their foundation? you replied, ‘The Deathless, Bhante.’”
“Excellent, excellent, Samiddhi!
It is well that you answer each question as it is asked; yet do not be conceited because of that.
The fourth.
