Sīhanādavagga Gaṇḍasutta “Monks, there are these nine kinds of boils. What nine? The boil of lust, the boil of hatred, the boil of delusion, the boil of anger, the boil of malice, the boil of denigration, the boil of insolence, the boil of envy, and the boil of miserliness. These, monks, are the nine kinds of boils.”
“Monks, suppose there were a boil that had been present for many years.
That boil would have nine openings and nine points of suppuration.”
Then, whatever might ooze out would be only impurity that oozes out, only a foul odor that oozes out, only something loathsome that oozes out;
whatever might be discharged...
It would produce only impurity; it would produce only a foul odor; it would produce only that which is loathsome.

"A boil," monks, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished by boiled rice and porridge, subject to impermanence, rubbing, massaging, breaking up, and dissolution.
Of that boil, there are nine openings, nine non-closing orifices.
Then, whatever oozes out is only impurity that oozes out, only a foul odor that oozes out, only something loathsome that oozes out;
whatever is emitted is likewise.
"It produces only impurity; it produces only foul odors; it produces only what is loathsome.
Therefore, monks, become disenchanted with this body.
(The fifth.)
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.16 2.

Sīhanādavagga Saññāsutta (The Discourse on Perceptions) “Monks, there are these nine perceptions. What nine? The perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a hacked-and-scattered corpse, the perception of a bleeding corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, and the perception of a skeleton. These, monks, are the nine perceptions.”
“Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their goal and the Deathless as their consummation.
What are the nine?”

“Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their goal and the Deathless as their consummation. They are: the perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion.
This is the sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.17 2.

Sīhanādavagga Kulasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of families that are difficult to approach. What four? The family that is miserly and stingy, yet gives alms; the family that is cruel and harsh, yet gives alms; the family that is ignorant and foolish, yet gives alms; and the family that is corrupt and depraved, yet gives alms. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of families that are difficult to approach.”

“Bhikkhus, possessing nine qualities, a family is not fit to be approached, or having been approached, it is not fit to sit down. What are the nine? [The text continues with the list of nine qualities.]”
They do not rise up for him in a pleasing manner; they do not pay him respectful salutation in a pleasing manner; they do not offer him a seat in a pleasing manner;
they conceal what he possesses; though there is much, they give him little; though it is excellent, they give him coarse food; they give without respect, not with respect;
they do not sit down near him to listen to the Dhamma; and they do not wish to hear what has been spoken by him.
“Monks, endowed with these nine qualities, a family is not fit to be approached, or if approached, it is not fit to sit down.
Endowed with what nine? Monks, endowed with these nine qualities, a family is fit to be approached, or if approached, it is fit to sit down.
With which nine?”
They rise up with courtesy; they salute with courtesy; they offer a seat with courtesy; they do not conceal what is available;
they give much even when there is much; they give fine things even when there are fine things; they give respectfully, not disrespectfully;
they sit down close by to listen to the Dhamma; they desire to hear what has been spoken.
“Bhikkhus, endowed with these nine factors, a family is worthy of being approached even if one has not yet been approached, and worthy of being sat with once approached.
The seventh. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 9.18

2. Sīhanādavagga Navaṅguposathasutta (AN 9.18, PTS AN iv 388) The Discourse on the Ninefold Uposatha "Monks, there are these nine factors that constitute the Uposatha. What nine? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells observing the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells observing feelings in feelings... He dwells observing mind in the mind... He dwells observing phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating impermanence in all conditioned phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating suffering in what is impermanent... He dwells contemplating non-self in what is suffering... He dwells contemplating disenchantment in what is non-self... He dwells contemplating fading away in what is disenchanted... He dwells contemplating cessation in what leads to fading away... He dwells contemplating relinquishment in what leads to cessation, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, monks, are the nine factors that constitute the Uposatha."
“Bhikkhus, when the Uposatha is observed endowed with nine factors, it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance.
And how, bhikkhus, is the Uposatha observed endowed with these nine factors so that it is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great radiance?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects thus:”

‘For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned the taking of life, abstain from taking life; they lay aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, they dwell full of kindness and sympathy for all living beings.

In this respect I emulate the Arahants, and my Uposatha will be observed.’

[as before] ... "For as long as life lasts, the Arahants, having abandoned high and luxurious beds and seats, abstain from high and luxurious beds and seats, and occupy low beds, either a small couch or a grass mat;

The Velāma Sutta (AN 9.20).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, does almsfood still continue to be given in your family?"
“Venerable sir, alms are given in my family;
however, they are coarse, consisting of broken rice with sour gruel as the second course.
“Householder, whether one gives coarse alms or refined ones, [it is still a gift].”
And he gives that gift without respect, without honoring it, not with his own hand, as something discarded,
and with the view that there is no future life. Wherever the fruit of that gift manifests,

his mind does not incline toward the enjoyment of excellent food, nor does his mind incline toward the enjoyment of excellent clothing, nor does his mind incline toward the enjoyment of excellent vehicles.
His mind does not incline toward the enjoyment of the five superior strands of sensual pleasure.
Even those whom he regards as sons, wives, slaves, messengers, or laborers do not wish to listen to him, do not lend an ear, and do not apply their minds to understand him.
For what reason?
For such, householder, is the result of actions performed without respect.
Whether one gives a coarse gift or a refined one, householder, if one gives it respectfully,
with a sense of honor, with one’s own hand, not by casting it away, and with the view that the gift will bear fruit in the future— then this is so.
Wherever the fruition of that particular gift arises, his mind inclines toward the enjoyment of sublime food,
his mind inclines toward the enjoyment of sublime clothing, his mind inclines toward the enjoyment of sublime vehicles,
and his mind inclines toward the enjoyment of the five sublime strands of sensual pleasure.
Even those who are one’s sons, daughters, slaves, messengers, or laborers listen attentively, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understand.
For what reason?
Because it is thus, householder, that the fruit of deeds performed with diligence comes to pass.
In the past, householder, there was a brahmin named Velāma.
He gave such a gift, a great gift:
he gave eighty-four thousand golden bowls filled with silver, and eighty-four thousand silver bowls.
He gave eighty-four thousand bowls filled with gold; he gave eighty-four thousand bronze vessels filled with silver;
he gave eighty-four thousand elephants adorned with golden trappings, bearing golden banners and covered with nets of gold;
and he gave eighty-four thousand chariots covered with lion skins, tiger skins, and leopard skins.
He gave eighty-four thousand elephants with trappings of white blankets, golden ornaments, and golden banners, covered with nets of gold;
he gave eighty-four thousand milch cows with calves, bound with fine linen and provided with bronze milking vessels;
he gave eighty-four thousand maidens adorned with earrings set with loose gems; and he gave eighty-four thousand couches spread with woolen rugs and covered with cotton quilts.
He gave eighty-four thousand sets of supreme antelope-hide rugs, spread with fine blankets, provided with upper covers, and furnished with red pillows at both ends;

drink, snacks, meals, dainties, and beverages.
The rivers, it seems, are overflowing.

"Surely Velāma the brahmin at that time was someone else; he gave that gift, that great gift. [But it was not so.]
But it should not be viewed in this way, householder.
At that time, I was the brahmin Velāma;

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.22 3. Sattāvāsavagga Assakhaḷuṅkasutta (The Wild Colt) “Bhikkhus, there are these nine abodes of beings. What nine?

(1) “There are beings that are different in body and different in perception, such as human beings, some devas, and some beings in the lower realms. This is the first abode of beings. (2) “There are beings that are different in body but identical in perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s company who are reborn through the first jhāna. This is the second abode of beings. (5) “There are beings that have attained the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the fifth abode of beings. (6) “There are beings that are non-percipient, possessed of a material body. This is the sixth abode of beings. (7) “There are beings that are percipient and possessed of a material body. This is the seventh abode of beings. “Monks, I will teach you about three wild colts, three wild men, three noble steeds among horses, three noble steeds among men, and three thoroughbred noble steeds, and three thoroughbred noble men.

"And what, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of wild colts?
Here, bhikkhus, one kind of wild colt is endowed with speed, but not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
But here, bhikkhus, another kind of wild colt is endowed with both speed and beauty, but not endowed with the right proportions of height and girth."
"But here, monks, a certain wild colt is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.

In this case, monks, a certain human wild colt possesses speed, but does not possess beauty, nor does he possess the right proportions of height and girth.
In this case, monks, another human wild colt possesses both speed and beauty, but does not possess the right proportions of height and girth.
In this case, monks, yet another human wild colt possesses speed, beauty, and the right proportions of height and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a wild colt endowed with speed, but not endowed with beauty, nor endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering"; he understands as it really is:
"This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, I say, is his speed.
But when questioned regarding the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he falters and does not answer.
This, I say, is not his excellence in appearance.
Furthermore, he does not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is not his excellence in physical stature and proportions.
"In this way, monks, a person who is like a wild colt possesses speed, but does not possess beauty or the excellence of physical proportions.
And how, monks, does a person who is like a wild colt possess both speed and beauty, but not the excellence of physical proportions?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … [and so on] … he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’"
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned on a matter concerning the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he provides an answer and does not falter.
This, I say, is his beauty.
Furthermore, he does not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his lack of physical stature and girth.
Thus, monks, the wild colt of a man possesses speed and possesses beauty, but does not possess physical stature and girth.
And how, monks, is a person like a wild colt endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?
Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: "This is suffering" ... [and so on] ... he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, I say, is his speed.
Furthermore, when questioned on matters of the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, he answers and does not falter;

Moreover, he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
This, I say, is his excellence of height and girth.
Thus, monks, the wild colt of a man is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with excellence of height and girth.
These, monks, are the three kinds of wild colts of men.
And what, monks, are the three kinds of excellent horses?
Here, monks, a certain excellent horse...
[as before] ...is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.
“Monks, these are the three noble steeds among horses.

He is endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth.

[as before] ...endowed with speed, endowed with beauty, and endowed with the right proportions of height and girth?
"Here, monks, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, a monk is of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.

“Bhikkhus, there are these nine abodes of beings. Which nine? [The text continues with the enumeration of the nine abodes.]”

This is the third abode of beings.
"There are, monks, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas.
This is the fourth abode of beings.
There are, monks, beings who are non-percipient and without experience, such as the Asaññasatta devas."
This is the fifth abode of beings.

There are, monks, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the sphere of infinite space.

3. Sattāvāsavagga Paññāsutta (AN 9.25, PTS AN iv 402) “Monks, there are these five abodes of beings. What five? There is the case where a certain person is not accomplished in virtue, not accomplished in concentration, and not accomplished in discernment. On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower realms, in hell. This is the first abode of beings. Then there is the case where a certain person is accomplished in virtue but not accomplished in concentration and not accomplished in discernment. On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the human world. This is the second abode of beings. Then there is the case where a certain person is accomplished in virtue and accomplished in concentration but not accomplished in discernment. On the dissolution of the body, after death, he reappears in the company of the devas of the Four Great Kings... the devas of the Thirty-three... the Yāma devas... the Tusita devas... the devas who delight in creation... the devas who control the creations of others... the devas of Brahmā’s retinue... the devas of Brahmā’s company. This is the seventh abode of beings. Then there is the case where a certain person is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in discernment. He, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life enters and dwells in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by discernment that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. This is the eighth abode of beings. These, monks, are the eight abodes of beings.”
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is well-sustained by wisdom, it is fitting for that bhikkhu to declare:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s mind well-sustained by wisdom?”
‘My mind is free from lust’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-familiarized;
‘My mind is free from hatred’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-familiarized;
‘My mind is free from delusion’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-familiarized.
“‘My mind is of a nature not subject to lust’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-fostered;
‘My mind is of a nature not subject to hatred’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-fostered;
‘My mind is of a nature not subject to delusion’—thus, by means of wisdom, the mind becomes well-fostered.”
‘My mind is no longer subject to relapse into existence in the sense-sphere realm,’ thus his mind is well-purified by wisdom;
‘My mind is no longer subject to relapse into existence in the fine-material sphere,’ thus his mind is well-purified by wisdom;
‘My mind is no longer subject to relapse into existence in the immaterial sphere,’ thus his mind is well-purified by wisdom.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind has been thoroughly developed by means of wisdom, it is fitting for that bhikkhu to declare:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This is the fifth [sutta].

A second time, the Venerable Candikāputta addressed the monks:

"And yet, friend Candikāputta, Devadatta teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus thus:

A third time, the Venerable Candikāputta addressed the bhikkhus:

And so, friend Candikaputta, Devadatta teaches the Dhamma to the bhikkhus in this way:"
“Friends, when a bhikkhu’s mind has been well-cultivated by means of the mind, it is fitting for that bhikkhu to declare:
‘I understand: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu’s mind well-cultivated by means of the mind?”
‘My mind is free from lust’—thus his mind is well cultivated by means of the mind;
‘My mind is free from hatred’—thus his mind is well cultivated by means of the mind;
‘My mind is free from delusion’—thus his mind is well cultivated by means of the mind.
‘My mind is of a nature not subject to lust,’ thus his mind is well-purified by the mind;
‘My mind is of a nature not subject to hatred,’ thus his mind is well-purified by the mind;
‘My mind is of a nature not subject to delusion,’ thus his mind is well-purified by the mind.
‘My mind is of a nature not to return to existence in the sense-sphere realm’—thus his mind is well-mastered by the mind;
‘My mind is of a nature not to return to existence in the form-sphere realm’—thus his mind is well-mastered by the mind;
‘My mind is of a nature not to return to existence in the formless-sphere realm’—thus his mind is well-mastered by the mind.
"Friend, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus rightly liberated, even if powerful forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of his vision, they do not overwhelm his mind.
His mind remains unmixed, established, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its vanishing.
It is just as if, friend, there were a stone pillar sixteen cubits long."
It has eight spokes below the rim and eight spokes above the rim.
Now, even if a violent wind and rain were to come from the eastern direction, it would neither shake nor tremble; and likewise from the western direction...
Then, if a violent wind and rain should come from the northern direction... or if a violent wind and rain should come from the southern direction, it would neither tremble nor shake.
For what reason?
“Because of its depth, friend, and because this stone pillar is firmly embedded.
In the same way, friend, when intense forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of vision of a bhikkhu whose mind is rightly liberated, they do not overwhelm his mind;
his mind remains unmixed, steady, and attained to imperturbability, and he contemplates its vanishing.”
Even if there are sounds cognizable by the ear that are terrifying… odors cognizable by the nose… flavors cognizable by the tongue…
“Tangible objects cognizable by the body...
mental phenomena cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, yet they do not overwhelm his mind;

The First Discourse on Enmity (Paṭhamaverasutta).
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One; having approached, he [saluted] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, when a noble disciple has stilled five fears and enmities and is endowed with the four factors of stream-entry, then, if he so desires, he may declare of himself:

'I am one for whom hell is exhausted, the animal realm is exhausted, the sphere of hungry ghosts is exhausted; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.'"
What are the five fears and enmities that have been stilled?
Householder, when one who destroys life, by reason of the destruction of life, generates fear and enmity pertaining to the present life,
and generates fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and experiences mental pain and dejection— [these are the first].
One who abstains from taking life generates neither fear nor enmity pertaining to the present life,
nor does he generate fear or enmity pertaining to future lives, nor does he experience mental pain or grief.
For one who abstains from taking life, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
Householder, one who takes what is not given...
one who engages in sexual misconduct... one who speaks falsehoods... [is reborn in hell].

One who indulges in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence produces fear and enmity pertaining to the present life, and produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives; one experiences mental pain and dejection.
One who abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence produces neither fear nor enmity pertaining to the present life... [and so forth].
One does not produce fear or enmity, nor does one produce fear or enmity pertaining to the future life,
nor does one experience mental pain or dejection.
For one who abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
These five fears and enmities are stilled.
"With how many factors of stream-entry is he endowed?
Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha: [text continues]"

‘Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He possesses verified confidence in the Dhamma:
‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise.’
He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha:

"The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing uprightly, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing correctly; that is to say, the four pairs of persons."

‘There are these eight types of persons; this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
“He possesses these four factors of stream-entry.
When, householder, these five fears and enmities have been stilled for a noble disciple, and he possesses these four factors of stream-entry, then, if he so desires, he may declare of himself:

‘I am one whose hell is exhausted, whose animal womb is exhausted, whose realm of hungry ghosts is exhausted; I am one whose states of deprivation, bad destinations, and perdition are exhausted. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my final goal.’”

The Second Discourse on Enmity (Dutiyaverasutta): “Bhikkhus,

It produces fear and enmity pertaining to future lives, and one experiences mental pain and dejection;
but for one who abstains from taking life...
[as before] ...in this way, that fear and enmity are stilled.
Monks, when one who takes what is not given ...

[and] one who indulges in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence, on account of that indulgence in fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence,

[He is likewise possessed of unwavering confidence] in the Dhamma... [and so on].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.29 3. Sattāvāsavagga Āghātavatthusutta (The Discourse on the Grounds for Resentment) “Monks, there are these nine grounds for resentment.

What nine? ‘He has treated me with hostility,’ this is the first ground for resentment. ‘He is treating me with hostility,’ this is the second ground for resentment. ‘He will treat me with hostility,’ this is the third ground for resentment. ‘He has treated someone dear to me with hostility,’ this is the fourth ground for resentment. ‘He is treating someone dear to me with hostility,’ this is the fifth ground for resentment. ‘He will treat someone dear to me with hostility,’ this is the sixth ground for resentment. ‘He has treated someone I dislike with kindness,’ this is the seventh ground for resentment. ‘He is treating someone I dislike with kindness,’ this is the eighth ground for resentment. ‘He will treat someone I dislike with kindness,’ this is the ninth ground for resentment. These, monks, are the nine grounds for resentment.”
“Monks, there are these nine grounds for resentment.
What are the nine?
‘He has done me harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He is doing me harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He will do me harm,’ one harbors resentment.
‘He has done what is harmful to one who is dear and pleasing to me’ … ‘He is doing what is harmful’ … ‘He will do what is harmful,’ thus one binds up resentment;
‘He has done what is beneficial for one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me’ … ‘he is doing what is beneficial’ … ‘he will do what is beneficial,’ one binds up resentment.
“Monks, these are the nine grounds for resentment.
Thus [ends] the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.30

3. Sattāvāsavagga Āghātapaṭivinayasutta (AN 9.30, PTS AN iv 408) “Monks, there are these seven abodes of beings. What seven? “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body and different in perception; this is the first abode of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body but identical in perception; this is the second abode of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body but different in perception; this is the third abode of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body and identical in perception; this is the fourth abode of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite space; this is the fifth abode of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth abode of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of nothingness; this is the seventh abode of beings. “These, monks, are the seven abodes of beings. “Furthermore, monks, there are these seven stations of consciousness. What seven? “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body and different in perception; this is the first station of consciousness. “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body but identical in perception; this is the second station of consciousness. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body but different in perception; this is the third station of consciousness. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body and identical in perception; this is the fourth station of consciousness. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite space; this is the fifth station of consciousness. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth station of consciousness. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of nothingness; this is the seventh station of consciousness. “These, monks, are the seven stations of consciousness. “Furthermore, monks, there are these seven final destinations of beings. What seven? “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body and different in perception; this is the first final destination of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are different in body but identical in perception; this is the second final destination of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body but different in perception; this is the third final destination of beings. “There are, monks, some beings who are identical in body and identical in perception; this is the fourth final destination of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite space; this is the fifth final destination of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth final destination of beings. “Then there are, monks, the beings of the realm of nothingness; this is the seventh final destination of beings. “These, monks, are the seven final destinations of beings. “Furthermore, monks, there are these seven noble ones. What seven? “There is, monks, the noble one who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. “There is, monks, the noble one who is a once-returner, who, having returned to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering. “There is, monks, the noble one who is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna in the interval. “There is, monks, the noble one who is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna upon landing. “There is, monks, the noble one who is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna without exertion. “There is, monks, the noble one who is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna with exertion.

“There is, monks, the noble one who is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “These, monks, are the seven noble ones. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how is it that one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “Monk, when one has abandoned three fetters—personality view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances—one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. “And how, monk, is one a once-returner, who, having returned to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering? When one has attenuated the fetters of sensual desire and ill will, one is a once-returner, who, having returned to this world only once more, will make an end of suffering. “And how, monk, is one a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna in the interval? When one has completely abandoned the five lower fetters, one is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna in the interval. “And how, monk, is one a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna upon landing? When one has completely abandoned the five lower fetters, one is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna upon landing. “And how, monk, is one a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna without exertion? When one has completely abandoned the five lower fetters, one is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna without exertion. “And how, monk, is one a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna with exertion? When one has completely abandoned the five lower fetters, one is a non-returner, who, having passed away from here, will attain parinibbāna with exertion. “And how, monk, is one an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge? When one has abandoned the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters, one is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. “Monk, when one has abandoned these seven things, one is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. And when one has abandoned these seven things, one is an arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that monk delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these seven ways of settling disputes. What seven? “There is, monks, a dispute that is settled by way of recollection. There is a dispute that is settled by way of a verdict of past insanity. There is a dispute that is settled by way of the majority. There is a dispute that is settled by way of the presence of the accused. There is a dispute that is settled by way of the majority of the Dhamma. There is a dispute that is settled by way of the majority of the Vinaya. There is a dispute that is settled by way of the admission of the fault. “And what, monks, is a dispute that is settled by way of recollection? Here, monks, in whatever monastery two bhikkhus have a dispute, and one of them says: ‘Friend, I recall that this matter was seen by you in such and such a way,’ and the other says: ‘I do not recall it, friend. Then, monks, that dispute is settled by way of recollection. This is called a dispute that is settled by way of recollection. “And what, monks, is a dispute that is settled by way of a verdict of past insanity? Here, monks, in whatever monastery two bhikkhus have a dispute, and one of them says: ‘Friend, I recall that this matter was seen by you in such and such a way,’
“Bhikkhus, there are these nine ways of removing resentment.
What are the nine?
One removes resentment by thinking: ‘He acted for my harm; what can be done about it?’”
‘He has acted for my harm; how could that be?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He will act for my harm; how could that be?’—thus one dispels resentment.
‘He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me... [and so on].
“He acted for my harm … [and so on] … ‘He will act for my harm; how could that be?’—thus he dispels resentment.
He acted for the benefit of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me … [and so on] …”
“He acts for the benefit of others…” [and so on] “…‘He will act for their benefit; how could such a thing happen?’—in this way he dispels resentment.
These, monks, are the nine ways of dispelling resentment.”
The Tenth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.31.
3. The Chapter on Abodes of Beings (Sattāvāsavagga).
The Discourse on Gradual Cessation (Anupubbanirodhasutta): “Monks,
there are these nine gradual cessations.”
Which nine?
For one who has attained the first jhāna, perceptions of sensual desire have ceased;
for one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought have ceased.
For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased;
for one who has attained the fourth jhāna, inhalation and exhalation have ceased;
for one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased.
For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has ceased;
for one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased.
For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, both perception and feeling have ceased.
These, monks, are the nine successive cessations.
The eleventh.
The third chapter: The Chapter on the Abodes of Beings.
Its summary verse:
The three states, the wild colt, craving, ...
Seventy-seven years of life;
two enmities and two hostilities,
through successive cessation— thus it is said.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.32 4. Mahāvagga Anupubbavihārasutta (The Discourse on the Gradual Abidings) “Monks, there are these nine gradual abidings and one gradual attainment. What are the nine? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the first jhāna, which is secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, and possesses applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he dwells having attained the second jhāna, which is internal serenity and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body; he dwells having attained the third jhāna, which the noble ones describe as ‘dwelling happily, equanimous and mindful. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he dwells having attained the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ he dwells having attained the base of infinite space. By completely surmounting the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he dwells having attained the base of infinite consciousness. By completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ he dwells having attained the base of nothingness. By completely surmounting the base of nothingness, he dwells having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. These, monks, are the nine gradual abidings. And what, monks, is the one gradual attainment? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the first jhāna... [as above] ...he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen this with wisdom, his mind is liberated from the taints. This, monks, is called the one gradual attainment.”
“Monks, there are these nine successive dwellings.
Which nine? [The text continues with the list of the nine successive dwellings.]”

The first jhāna, the second jhāna, the third jhāna, the fourth jhāna, the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the cessation of perception and feeling—
these, monks, are the nine successive dwellings. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.33 4. Mahāvagga Anupubbavihārasamāpattisutta (The Discourse on the Attainments of Successive Dwellings) “Monks, there are these nine successive dwellings. What nine? (1) “Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

(2) “With the subsiding of thought and examination, he dwells having attained the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration. (3) “With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body; he dwells having attained the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwelling happily. (4) “With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he dwells having attained the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. (5) “By completely transcending forms, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ he dwells having attained the base of infinite space. (6) “By completely transcending the base of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he dwells having attained the base of infinite consciousness. (7) “By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] ‘there is nothing,’ he dwells having attained the base of nothingness. (8) “By completely transcending the base of nothingness, he dwells having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. (9) “By completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he dwells having attained the cessation of perception and feeling. These, monks, are the nine successive dwellings.”
“Monks, I will teach you these nine successive attainments of dwelling; listen to that...
What, monks, are the nine successive attainments of dwelling?

"Wherever sensual desires cease, and those who, having repeatedly ceased sensual desires, dwell [therein]— surely those venerable ones, by that very factor, are hungerless, extinguished, crossed over, and have gone to the further shore," I say. "If someone were to say,
'I do not know where sensual desires cease, nor do I see those who, having repeatedly ceased sensual desires, dwell [therein],' then he should be told this:"

“Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
It is here that sensual pleasures cease; and having repeatedly brought those sensual pleasures to cessation, they dwell [therein].
Surely, bhikkhus, one who is not fraudulent and not deceitful would welcome this statement and rejoice in it, saying, “Excellent!”
Having rejoiced and delighted in what was said, one should pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

Wherever initial and sustained thought cease, and wherever those who have repeatedly brought initial and sustained thought to cessation dwell, I say: "Surely those venerable ones are hungerless, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the further shore in that respect.
"Where do initial and sustained thought cease? And who are those who, having repeatedly brought initial and sustained thought to cessation, dwell [therein]?"
‘I do not know this; I do not see this. To one who speaks thus, it should be said:
‘Friend, here a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna;
herein applied and sustained thought cease, and having repeatedly ceased those applied and sustained thoughts, he dwells [therein].’”
"Truly, monks, one who is not deceitful and not guileful would welcome and rejoice in what is well-spoken, saying, 'Excellent!
Having welcomed and rejoiced in what is well-spoken, he would pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

Wherever rapture ceases, and those who, having repeatedly brought rapture to cessation, dwell [therein]—I say that those venerable ones are truly free from craving, extinguished, crossed over, and gone beyond in that respect."
‘Where does rapture cease, and who, having repeatedly ceased rapture, dwell [therein]—I do not know this, I do not see this,’ if anyone should speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
‘In this case, friend, through the fading away of rapture... a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the third jhāna.’
‘Herein, rapture ceases, and they dwell having repeatedly brought that rapture to cessation.
Monks, a person who is honest and free from deceit would certainly welcome and rejoice in these words, saying, ‘Excellent!
Having welcomed and rejoiced in these words, he would pay homage and attend upon them with palms joined in reverence.

“Wherever equanimity-and-bliss ceases, and whoever dwell having repeatedly ceased equanimity-and-bliss, I say of them: ‘Surely those venerable ones are hungerless, extinguished, crossed over, and gone to the further shore in that respect.
If someone were to say: ‘I do not know, I do not see where equanimity-and-bliss ceases, nor who dwell having repeatedly ceased equanimity-and-bliss,’ he should be told this:”
‘Here, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
herein equanimity and pleasure cease, and they dwell having repeatedly brought about the cessation of that equanimity and pleasure.
Surely, bhikkhus, one who is not fraudulent and not deceitful would welcome such speech and rejoice in it, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
Having rejoiced and delighted in what was said, one should pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

Wherever perception of form ceases, and whoever dwell having repeatedly ceased perception of form, I say of them: “Truly, those venerable ones are insatiable-free, extinguished, crossed over, and gone beyond in that respect.
“Where does perception of form cease, and who are those who dwell having repeatedly ceased perception of form?”
‘I do not know this; I do not see this. To one who speaks thus, he should be addressed as follows:

‘Friend, here a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that “space is infinite,” enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
It is here that perceptions of form cease. And they, having repeatedly ceased those perceptions of form, dwell [in that state].’”
“Indeed, monks, one who is not deceitful and not fraudulent would welcome and rejoice in what is well-spoken;
having welcomed and rejoiced in what is well-spoken, he would pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

Wherever the perception of the base of infinite space ceases, and those who, having repeatedly brought that perception of the base of infinite space to cessation, dwell [therein]—‘Surely those venerable ones are insatiable-free, extinguished, crossed over, and gone to the further shore in that respect,’ I say.”
‘Where does the perception of the base of infinite space cease, and who, having repeatedly ceased the perception of the base of infinite space, dwell [therein]—this I do not know;
this I do not see,’ one who should speak thus should be addressed as follows:
‘In this case, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking “consciousness is infinite,” enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.’”
‘Here the perception of the base of infinite space ceases, and they dwell having repeatedly brought that perception of the base of infinite space to cessation.
Surely, bhikkhus, one who is not fraudulent and not deceitful would say ‘Excellent! and would rejoice and approve of what was said;
having rejoiced and approved of what was said, he would pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

"Wherever the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases, and wherever those who dwell having repeatedly ceased the perception of the base of infinite consciousness abide— in that respect, I say, 'Surely those venerable ones are free from hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and gone to the further shore. If someone were to say,

'I do not know where the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases, nor whom I see who dwell having repeatedly ceased the perception of the base of infinite consciousness,' he should be told this:"
‘Here, friends, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking “there is nothing,” enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Herein, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness ceases; and they dwell having repeatedly ceased that perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
Surely, bhikkhus, one who is not deceitful and not fraudulent would welcome this speech and approve of it, saying: ‘Excellent!’”
Having rejoiced and delighted in what was said, one should pay homage with palms joined and attend upon them.

Wherever the perception of the base of nothingness ceases, and whoever dwell having repeatedly ceased the perception of the base of nothingness, I say: "Truly, those venerable ones are insatiable-free, extinguished, crossed over, and have gone to the further shore in that respect.
"Where does the perception of the base of nothingness cease, and who are those who dwell having repeatedly ceased the perception of the base of nothingness?"
If someone were to say, ‘I do not know this; I do not see this,’ he should be told:
‘In this case, friend, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is here that the perception of the base of nothingness ceases, and they dwell having repeatedly ceased that perception of the base of nothingness.’”
"Indeed, monks, one who is not deceitful and not fraudulent would welcome and rejoice in what is well-spoken;
having welcomed and rejoiced in what is well-spoken, he would pay homage with palms joined and attend upon it.
Wherever the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ceases, and those [who have attained] the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception..."

"Having repeatedly brought about the cessation of [the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception], they dwell therein; I say that those venerable ones are certainly free from hunger, extinguished, crossed over, and have reached the further shore in that respect.
Where does the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception cease, and who, having repeatedly brought about its cessation, dwell therein?"
If someone were to say, ‘I do not know this; I do not see this,’ he should be told:
‘In this case, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.

It is here that the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ceases; and they dwell having repeatedly brought about the cessation of that perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.’”
“Indeed, bhikkhus, one who is not deceitful and not fraudulent would welcome and rejoice in what is well-spoken;
having welcomed and rejoiced in what is well-spoken, he would pay homage and attend upon it with palms joined.
These, bhikkhus, are the nine successive attainments of dwelling.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.34 4. Mahāvagga
The Discourse on the Happiness of Nibbāna (Nibbānasukhasutta).
At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“This Nibbāna, friends, is bliss.
This Nibbāna, friends, is bliss.”
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“But what, friend Sāriputta, is the happiness here that there is no feeling here?
“This itself, friend, is the happiness here: that there is no feeling here.”
"Friends, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure.
What are the five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust— these, friends, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on these five strands of sensual pleasure, this, friends, is called sensual pleasure.
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
If, while that bhikkhu is dwelling in this state, perceptions and mental applications accompanied by sensual desire occur to him, that is an affliction for him.
Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would be only as an affliction."
In the same way, those perceptions and mental engagements associated with sensual pleasures continue to occur for him. This is a sickness for him.
And whatever is a sickness, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, too, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.
Furthermore, friends, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
If, while that bhikkhu dwells in this state, perceptions and mental explorations accompanied by applied thought occur to him, that is an affliction for him.
Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would be only as an affliction.
In the same way, those perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by applied thought continue to occur for him. This becomes an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.
Furthermore, friends, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the third jhāna...

If, while that bhikkhu dwells in this state, perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by rapture still occur, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would be only as an affliction; so too, friends, if perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by rapture still occur for a bhikkhu dwelling in this state, that is an affliction for him.
In the same way, those perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by rapture arise in him. That indeed becomes an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.
Furthermore, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

If, while that bhikkhu dwells in this state, perceptions and mental engagements associated with equanimity occur to him, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise in one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction; so too, friends, if perceptions and mental engagements associated with equanimity occur to that bhikkhu while he dwells in this state, that is an affliction for him.
In the same way, when perceptions and mental attentions accompanied by equanimity occur to him, that becomes an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, too, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is happiness.

Furthermore, friends, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, [perceiving] "space is infinite.

If, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, perceptions and mental engagements associated with form should still occur, that is an affliction for him. Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would be only as an affliction; so too, friends, if perceptions and mental engagements associated with form should occur for that bhikkhu while he dwells in this dwelling, that is an affliction for him.
In the same way, those perceptions and mental attentions associated with form still occur for him. That is an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, too, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.
Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, a bhikkhu, aware that "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.

If, while that bhikkhu is dwelling in this state, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space still occur, that is a source of affliction for him. Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction; so too, friends, if perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space still occur for that bhikkhu dwelling in this state, that is a source of affliction for him.
In the same way, those perceptions and mental attentions associated with the base of infinite space arise in him. That is an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.
Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
If, while that bhikkhu is dwelling in this state, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite consciousness still occur, that is an affliction for him.
Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction.
In the same way, when perceptions and mental attentions associated with the base of infinite consciousness occur to him, that becomes an affliction for him.
Now, friends, what is called an affliction has been described by the Blessed One as suffering.
It is by this method, friends, that it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of nothingness still occur, that is an affliction for him.
Just as, friends, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction.
In the same way, those perceptions and mental attentions associated with the base of nothingness occur to him. That is an affliction for him.
And whatever is an affliction, friends, that has been called suffering by the Blessed One.
By this method, friends, it should be understood how Nibbāna is blissful.

"Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
It is in this way, too, friends, that it should be understood how Nibbāna is bliss.
This was the third [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.35 4. Mahāvagga Gāvīupamāsutta – The Simile of the Cow “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a cowherd who was unskilled and incompetent, who did not know the pastures, the watering holes, or the resting places. He would drive the cattle out to pasture at the wrong time, let them drink water at the wrong time, and make them rest at the wrong time.

As a result, that herd of cattle would not grow, increase, or flourish. Why is that? Because of the cowherd’s lack of skill and incompetence. In the same way, bhikkhus, there are five factors of striving that are unskillful and unbeneficial. What five? Here, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He dwells with his mind obsessed by dullness and drowsiness, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen dullness and drowsiness. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, and he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five factors of striving that are unskillful and unbeneficial. Suppose there were a cowherd who was skilled and competent, who knew the pastures, the watering holes, and the resting places. He would drive the cattle out to pasture at the right time, let them drink water at the right time, and make them rest at the right time. As a result, that herd of cattle would grow, increase, and flourish. Why is that? Because of the cowherd’s skill and competence. In the same way, bhikkhus, there are five factors of striving that are skillful and beneficial. What five? Here, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind unobsessed by sensual lust, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with a mind unobsessed by ill will, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He dwells with a mind unobsessed by dullness and drowsiness, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen dullness and drowsiness. He dwells with a mind unobsessed by restlessness and remorse, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with a mind unobsessed by doubt, and he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five factors of striving that are skillful and beneficial.”
“Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mountain cow, foolish, incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled in roaming over a rugged mountain.
It might think to itself: [as in the full sutta]”
‘What if I were to go to a direction never before visited, eat grass never before eaten, and drink water never before drunk?
She would not have firmly planted her forefoot before lifting up her hind foot.
Thus she would neither go to a direction never before visited, nor eat grass never before eaten, nor drink water never before drunk.
And while standing in that place, she might think:
“What if I were to go to a direction never before visited, eat grass never before eaten, and drink water never before drunk? Yet she would not return safely from that place. Why is that?
For just as that mountain cow, bhikkhus, was foolish, incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled in roaming over the rugged mountains, even so, bhikkhus, here a certain bhikkhu is foolish,
incompetent, ignorant of the terrain, and unskilled; yet, secluded from sensual pleasures,
secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
He enters and dwells in that jhāna;
yet he does not cultivate, develop, or repeatedly practice that sign, nor does he resolve upon it with firm determination.
This thought occurs to him:

‘What if, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration?
Yet he is unable to enter and dwell in the second jhāna...
It occurs to him:

‘What if I, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, were to enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion?
Yet he is unable to enter and dwell in the first jhāna, secluded from sensual pleasures...

This, monks, is called a monk who has fallen away from both sides, who has slipped from both sides, just like that foolish, incompetent, inexperienced, and unskilled mountain cow who wanders on the rugged mountains.”
“Just as, monks, there might be a mountain cow that is wise, experienced, discerning, and skilled in roaming over rugged mountains.
It would think to itself:
‘What if I were to go to a region never before visited, eat grass never before tasted, and drink water never before drunk?’”
Having firmly planted her forefoot, she would lift up her hind foot;
she would go toward a direction never before traversed, eat grasses never before eaten, and drink waters never before drunk.
And in whatever place she stood, it would occur to her thus:
‘What if I were to go to a region never before visited, eat grass never before eaten, and drink water never before drunk,’ and then return safely to that same place.
Why is that? Because, monks, that mountain cow is wise, clever, experienced, and skilled in roaming over the rugged mountains.”
In the same way, monks, here a certain bhikkhu who is wise, competent, knowledgeable of the field, and skillful,

secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
Thus he cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign; he makes it well-established and resolves upon it.
It occurs to him:

“What if, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna, which is internal tranquility and singleness of mind, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and filled with rapture and happiness?”
Thus, without disturbing the second jhāna, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
He cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign, and he resolves upon it with firm resolve.
It occurs to him:
‘What if, with the fading away of rapture, I were to dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending,
and experience happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say: “He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous”—
thus entering upon and dwelling in the third jhāna?’
Thus, without abandoning the third jhāna, through the fading away of rapture, he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
He cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign, and he establishes it firmly.
It occurs to him:

‘What if, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I were to enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity?
Without wavering from the fourth jhāna, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
He cultivates that sign, develops it, makes much of it, and firmly resolves upon it.
It occurs to him:

“What if, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ I were to enter and dwell in the base of infinite space?
Without transgressing the base of infinite space, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form... he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Thus he pursues that sign, develops it, cultivates it repeatedly, and firmly resolves upon it.
It occurs to him:
"What if I, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, were to enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'consciousness is infinite'?"

Thus, without harming the base of infinite consciousness, having completely transcended the base of infinite space, he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] "consciousness is infinite.
He cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign, and maintains it firmly resolved.
It occurs to him thus:
‘What if I, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking “there is nothing,” were to enter and dwell in the base of nothingness?
Without violating the base of nothingness, he completely transcends the base of infinite consciousness and, thinking “there is nothing,” enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
He cultivates, develops, and multiplies that sign; he establishes it firmly.
It occurs to him:
“What if I, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, were to enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Without striving for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he completely transcends the base of nothingness and enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
He cultivates that sign, develops it, makes much of it, and firmly resolves upon it.
It occurs to him:
“What if I, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, were to enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling?”

Thus, without forcing the cessation of perception and feeling, he completely transcends the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and dwells having entered upon the cessation of perception and feeling.
When, monks, a monk both enters and emerges from that very attainment, his mind becomes pliant and wieldy.
With a pliant and wieldy mind, concentration becomes immeasurable and well-developed.

Thus, when immeasurable concentration has been well developed, whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he inclines his mind toward for the sake of realizing through direct knowledge, he attains the capability of being a witness therein, in each respective sphere.

If he should wish: "May I exercise the various kinds of psychic power—I, being one, may become many; being many, may I become one... [and so on] up to exercising mastery with the body as far as the Brahma-world," he attains it.
In each and every case, he attains the state of being capable of realization whenever there is a suitable occasion.
If he so desires: "With the divine ear-element … [as before] … whenever there is a suitable occasion."
Thus, if he so desires: “May I, by encompassing with my own mind the minds of other beings and other persons, understand them;
may I understand a mind affected by lust as a mind affected by lust, and a mind free from lust as a mind free from lust.”
One should know a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred," one should know a mind free from hatred as "a mind free from hatred," and one should know a deluded mind as "a deluded mind."
a mind free from delusion … a contracted mind … a distracted mind …
or a developed mind … or an undeveloped mind … or a surpassable mind …
Whether the mind is unsurpassed, or concentrated, or unconcentrated...
‘May I understand a liberated mind as a liberated mind,
or an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ one attains the capability of being a witness in each and every instance where there is a suitable basis.

Thus, if he wishes: "May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births... [as before]... thus may I recollect my manifold past lives with their modes and details," he attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is a suitable basis.

If he wishes: "With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... [as before]... may I know beings passing away and being reborn according to their karma," he attains the capacity for realization in each respective case, whenever there is a suitable basis.
In each and every case, he attains the capacity for realization in whatever sphere there may be.

If he should wish: "May I, through the destruction of the taints, dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom," then in each and every case, he attains the capacity for realization in whatever sphere there may be.
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.36 4. Mahāvagga
The Jhāna Sutta (AN 9.36, PTS AN iv 422):
“Bhikkhus, I say that even by relying on the first jhāna, there is the destruction of the taints.”
“Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the second jhāna;
I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the third jhāna;
I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the fourth jhāna.”
“Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the base of infinite space;
I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the base of infinite consciousness;
I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the base of nothingness.”
“Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the cessation of perception and feeling.
‘Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints occurs by depending on the first jhāna,’ so it was said.”
And with reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as above] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
Whatever there is therein of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—
He contemplates those phenomena as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien,
as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having turned the mind away from those states, he directs the mind toward the deathless element, thinking:
"This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there,
not subject to return from that world. Just as, monks, an archer or an archer’s apprentice,
having practiced on a straw man or a heap of clay, at a later time becomes a long-distance shooter, a sharp-shooter, and one who can pierce a great body;
In the same way, monks, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...a monk enters and dwells in the first jhāna.

Whatever there is therein that pertains to form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—those phenomena he regards as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a misfortune, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating.
He contemplates them as empty and as non-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having withdrawn his mind from those phenomena, he directs his mind toward the deathless element:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
“Bhikkhus, when I said: ‘Depending on the first jhāna, I declare the destruction of the taints,’ it was with reference to this that I said this. And when I said:
‘Depending on the second jhāna…’ [and so on].”
“Monks, relying on the third jhāna... [and so on] ...

‘Monks, relying on the fourth jhāna, I declare the destruction of the taints,’ thus it was said. With reference to what was this said? [The Buddha then describes the process of attaining the fourth jhāna and the subsequent realization of the four noble truths, leading to the destruction of the taints.
Thus it was said, and with reference to this it was said.”

Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Whatever there is therein that belongs to form, that belongs to feeling, that belongs to perception, that belongs to volitional formations, or that belongs to consciousness—
He contemplates those phenomena as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien,
