as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having turned the mind away from those phenomena, he directs the mind toward the deathless element, thinking:
“This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final nibbāna there,
not subject to return from that world. Just as, monks, an archer or an archer’s apprentice,
having practiced on a straw man or a mound of clay, at a later time becomes one who shoots from afar, one who pierces the mark, and one who splits a great body;
In the same way, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
Whatever there is therein that pertains to form, pertains to feeling... [as above] ...he is no longer subject to returning from that world.
“Bhikkhus, I say that by depending on the fourth jhāna, there is the destruction of the taints. This is what was said; and with reference to this it was said.
“Bhikkhus, I say that by depending on the base of infinite space, there is the destruction of the taints. This too was said;
and with reference to what was it said?

“Here, monks, by completely transcending perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and by non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness— those phenomena he regards as impermanent,
as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, and as empty.”
He regards them as not-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having withdrawn his mind from those phenomena, he directs his mind toward the deathless element:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to return from that world.
“Just as, monks, an archer or an archer’s apprentice, having practiced on a straw man or a mound of clay, at a later time becomes one who shoots from afar,
one who pierces the mark, and one who splits a great body; even so, monks,

with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite.’”
Thus, whatever there is therein belonging to feeling, belonging to perception...
[and so on] ...he is of a nature not to return from that world.
"Bhikkhus, depending even upon the base of infinite space, I declare the destruction of the taints."
Thus, that which was said— "Bhikkhus,
depending even on the base of infinite consciousness...
depending even on the base of nothingness, I declare the destruction of the taints"— it is with reference to this that it was said.
And with reference to what was this said?
Here, monks, a monk, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—those phenomena...
He contemplates them as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, and as non-self.
He turns his mind away from those phenomena.
Having turned the mind away from those phenomena, he directs his mind toward the deathless element, thinking:
“This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not reach the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma and that delight in the Dhamma, with the total destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there,
not subject to return from that world. Just as, bhikkhus, an archer or an archer’s apprentice,
having practiced on a straw man or a mound of clay, at a later time becomes a long-distance shooter, a sharp-shooter, and one who can pierce a great body;
In the same way, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [a monk] enters and dwells in the base of nothingness,
perceiving "there is nothing. Whatever there is therein that pertains to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— those phenomena he regards as impermanent,
as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as a calamity, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, and as empty.
He regards them as non-self.
He withdraws his mind from those phenomena.
Having withdrawn his mind from those phenomena, he directs his mind toward the deathless element:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Established therein, he attains the destruction of the taints.

If he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then by that very passion for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the total exhaustion of the five lower fetters, he becomes one of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, no longer subject to return from that world.
‘I say that even by depending on the base of nothingness, there is the destruction of the taints’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this. Thus, monks,
to whatever extent there is attainment of perception, to that extent there is penetration to final knowledge.
"But as for these two bases, monks, which depend on these [preceding states]—
the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the cessation of perception and feeling—
I say that they are to be rightly proclaimed by meditators who are skilled in attainments and skilled in emerging from attainments, after having entered them and emerged from them."
The Fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.37. 4. Mahāvagga.
The Ānanda Sutta (AN 9.37).
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus.
"Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda said this:
“It is wonderful, friends! It is marvelous, friends!
To what extent the opening has been attained within such confinement by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One!”
It has been fully awakened for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief,
for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
Such an eye as that shall come to be, and those forms shall exist, yet one shall not experience that sense-sphere.
There will indeed be that very ear for you and those sounds, yet you will not experience that sense-base.
There will indeed be that very nose for you and those odors, yet you will not experience that sense-base.
There will indeed be that very tongue for you and those flavors, yet you will not experience that sense-base.
“Then there will be a body called ‘silver’ and tactile objects, yet you will not experience that sense base.
When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend Ānanda, does one who possesses perception not experience that sense base, or rather, one who is without perception?”
“Friend, one who is percipient experiences that sphere, not one who is non-percipient.
“But what does one who is percipient experience in that sphere?

“Here, friend, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [thinking] ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.”
"Even with such a perception, friend, he does not experience that sphere.
Furthermore, friend, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking 'consciousness is infinite,' enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
Even with such a perception, friend, he does not experience that sphere."
"Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving] 'there is nothing,' a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
Even though he has such a perception, friends, he does not experience that base as such.
Friends, on one occasion I was dwelling at Sāketa in the Añjana Grove, the Deer Park."
Then, friends, the bhikkhunī Jaṭilavāsikā approached me; having approached, she paid homage to me and stood to one side. Standing to one side, friends, the bhikkhunī Jaṭilavāsikā said this to me:

“Venerable Ānanda, that concentration which is neither bent forward nor bent backward, and which has not gone to the state of being restrained by volitional effort, is steady because of its liberation;
it is content because of its steadiness; and it does not tremble because of its contentment.”
“Venerable Ānanda, what fruit has this concentration been said by the Blessed One to have?
When this was said, friend, I said to the bhikkhunī Jaṭilavāsikā:
“Sister, that concentration which is neither leaning forward nor leaning back, and which does not proceed by means of suppression through volitional effort—”
“Because of being liberated, he is established; because of being established, he is content; because of being content, he does not tremble.
This concentration, sister, has been called ‘having final knowledge as its fruit’ by the Blessed One.
“Even while perceiving thus, friend, one does not experience that sphere.”
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.38. 4. Mahāvagga.
The Discourse to the Materialists (Lokāyatikasutta).
Then two brahmins who were materialists approached the Blessed One; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those brahmins said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, Pūraṇa Kassapa claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, to possess knowledge and vision without exception, saying:
'Whether I am walking or standing, asleep or awake, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously present to me.'"
Thus he says:
‘I dwell knowing and seeing the infinite world with infinite knowledge.
Master Gotama, this Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta also claims to be all-knowing and all-seeing, and to possess knowledge and vision without remainder.
‘Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking, knowledge and vision are constantly and continuously established before me.
He says thus:
‘I dwell knowing and seeing the infinite world with infinite knowledge.’
“Master Gotama, between these two proponents of knowledge, both of whom speak in opposition to one another, who speaks the truth and who speaks falsehood?
“Enough, brahmins.
Let this matter rest.”
“Between these two proponents of knowledge, who speak in opposition to one another, who speaks the truth and who speaks falsehood?
Brahmins, I shall teach you the Dhamma;
listen to it and attend closely, and I will speak.”
“Yes, sir,” those brahmins replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Brahmins, it is just as if four men were standing in the four directions, endowed with supreme speed and a supreme stride.”
They would be endowed with such speed, just as if a skilled archer, trained, practiced, and experienced, were to shoot a light arrow across the shadow of a palm tree without difficulty;
and they would have such a stride, just as if a man standing in the eastern ocean were to say: "The western ocean is [only this far away]."
‘I shall reach the end of the world by traveling.
Yet, apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; apart from the business of defecation and urination;

and apart from dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—even if he were one hundred years old, living for a hundred years, and traveled for a hundred years—he would die along the way without ever reaching the end of the world.
Then a man standing in the western direction...
[and so on] ...then a man standing in the northern direction...
then a man standing in the southern direction might say this:
‘I shall reach the end of the world by traveling.
Yet, apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; apart from the business of defecation and urination;

and apart from dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—even if he were one with a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, and traveled for a hundred years—he would die along the way without ever reaching the end of the world.
And why is that? Brahmins, I do not say that the end of the world is to be known, seen, or reached by such a running about.
Nor, Brahmins, do I say that there is a making an end of suffering without reaching the end of the world.
"Brahmins, these five strands of sensual pleasure are called 'the world' in the discipline of the Noble One.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust:
these, brahmins, are called the five cords of sensual pleasure in the discipline of the Noble One.

Here, brahmins, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“Brahmins, this is called a bhikkhu who, having reached the end of the world, dwells at the end of the world.
Others say of him:
‘He too is included within the world; he too has not escaped from the world.’”
“Brahmins, I too say this:
‘This, too, is included within the world; this, too, has not escaped from the world.
Furthermore, brahmins, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...”
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna. This,
brahmins, is called a bhikkhu who, having come to the end of the world, dwells at the end of the world.
Others said this about him:
"He too is included within the world; he too has not escaped from the world. For I too, brahmins, speak thus: [he is included within the world; he too has not escaped from the world].
‘This too is included within the world; this too has not escaped from the world.

Furthermore, brahmins, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, brahmins, is called a bhikkhu who, having come to the end of the world, dwells at the end of the world.
Others say this of him:
"He too is included within the world; he too has not escaped from the world. For I too, brahmins, speak thus: [he is included within the world; he has not escaped from the world].
‘This too is included within the world; this too has not escaped from the world.

Furthermore, brahmins, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness… having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness… [and so on].”
By completely transcending the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This, brahmins, is called a bhikkhu who, having come to the end of the world, dwells at the end of the world.
Others said this to him:
‘This too is included within the world; this too has not escaped from the world.
For I too, brahmins, say:
‘This too is included within the world; this too has not escaped from the world.’

"Furthermore, brahmins, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
This, brahmins, is called a bhikkhu who, having reached the end of the world, dwells at the end of the world, having crossed over attachment to the world.
Thus ends the seventh [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.39 4. Mahāvagga Devāsurasaṅgāmasutta (The Discourse on the Battle between the Devas and Asuras) “Bhikkhus, there was once a battle between the devas and the asuras. In that battle, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated. Then, the asuras, being defeated, fled in all directions. Some asuras fled toward the east, some toward the south, some toward the west, and some toward the north. ‘The devas have won this battle; we have been defeated,’ they thought. Then, bhikkhus, the asuras who had fled toward the east saw the eastern quarter ablaze, burning, and glowing with flames. They were terrified, seized by fear, and their hair stood on end. They cried out: ‘We are lost! We are finished!

Then, bhikkhus, the asuras who had fled toward the south saw the southern quarter ablaze, burning, and glowing with flames... [and so on for the west and north]. Then, bhikkhus, the asuras who had fled toward the nadir saw the nadir ablaze, burning, and glowing with flames. They were terrified, seized by fear, and their hair stood on end. They cried out: ‘We are lost! We are finished! Then, bhikkhus, the asuras who had fled toward the zenith saw the zenith ablaze, burning, and glowing with flames. They were terrified, seized by fear, and their hair stood on end. They cried out: ‘We are lost! We are finished! Then, bhikkhus, the devas said to those asuras: ‘Why, friends, are you terrified, seized by fear, and your hair standing on end? ‘Friends, we see the eastern quarter ablaze, burning, and glowing with flames... [and so on for the other directions]. ‘But, friends, this is not the eastern quarter; it is the gateway to the asuras. This is not the southern quarter... [and so on for the other directions]. ‘Friends, this is the gateway to the asuras. Then, bhikkhus, the asuras, having heard the words of the devas, emerged from the gateway to the asuras and entered the gateway to the devas. Having entered the gateway to the devas, they stood there. Then, bhikkhus, the devas said to those asuras: ‘Come, friends, welcome, friends! You are our kin, friends; you are our relatives, friends. What is it that you desire, friends? What can we do for you? ‘Friends, let us be your servants. ‘But, friends, we are the devas, and you are the asuras. How could we be your servants? ‘Friends, let us be your vassals. ‘But, friends, we are the devas, and you are the asuras. How could we be your vassals? ‘Friends, let us pay you tribute. ‘But, friends, we are the devas, and you are the asuras. How could we receive tribute from you? ‘Friends, let us go to you for refuge. ‘Well then, friends, go for refuge to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Then, bhikkhus, the asuras went to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and having approached him, they paid homage to him and sat down at one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma. Having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, those asuras, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on their right, departed. Then, bhikkhus, those asuras, having gone to the devas, paid homage to them and stood at one side. As they were standing there, the devas said to those asuras: ‘Friends, where did you come from? ‘Friends, we went to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. ‘And what did the Blessed One say to you? ‘Friends, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened us with a discourse on the Dhamma. Then, bhikkhus, the devas said to those asuras: ‘Friends, go again to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and having approached him, pay homage to him with your heads at his feet in my name, saying: “Venerable sir, the devas pay homage to the Blessed One with their heads at his feet. And say this: “Venerable sir, let the Blessed One come to the devas; let the Fortunate One come to the devas, out of compassion. Then, bhikkhus, those asuras, having gone to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, paid homage to him with their heads at his feet and stood at one side. As they were standing there, they said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable sir, the devas pay homage to the Blessed One with their heads at his feet. Venerable sir, let the Blessed One come to the devas; let the Fortunate One come to the devas, out of compassion. Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One, having understood the asuras’ request, set out for the devas. Just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm, even so the Blessed One vanished from the human world and appeared among the devas. Then, bhikkhus, the devas, seeing the Blessed One coming from afar, prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat and washed his feet. The devas also washed the Blessed One’s feet with scented water. When the Blessed One’s feet were washed, a great stream of water flowed out from beneath the seat, which then divided into four channels and disappeared into the earth. Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the devas with a discourse on the Dhamma. Having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, the devas, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, paid homage to the Blessed One and kept him on their right, departing. Then, bhikkhus, the Blessed One, having lived among the devas for as long as he wished, vanished from the world of the devas and reappeared in Jambudīpa, just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm.”
“Bhikkhus, once in the past a battle had been arrayed between the devas and the asuras.
In that battle, bhikkhus, the asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated.”
And the Parājita gods, monks, retreated facing north, while the asuras attacked.
Then, monks, it occurred to the gods:
“The asuras are indeed attacking us.”
"Perhaps we shall engage in battle with the asuras a second time.
And a second time, monks, the devas engaged in battle with the asuras.
And a second time, monks, the asuras alone were victorious, and the devas were defeated.
And the Parājita devas, monks, retreated facing north, while the asuras prevailed.
Then, monks, it occurred to the devas:
"The asuras are indeed prevailing."
"Perhaps we shall engage in battle with the asuras even for a third time.
And for a third time, monks, the devas engaged in battle with the asuras.
For a third time, monks, the asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated.
"Monks, the defeated devas, being afraid, entered Devapura itself.
And once they had reached Devapura, monks, it occurred to those devas:
'Now we dwell with ourselves having gone to a place of safety for the fearful; we are no longer subject to the asuras.'"
“Bhikkhus, it occurred to the asuras as well:
‘The gods are now dwelling under the protection of those who are fearful; they are no longer open to attack by us.
Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a battle had been arrayed between the gods and the asuras.”
In that battle, monks, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
Having been defeated, monks, the asuras fled toward the south, while the devas pursued them.
Then, monks, it occurred to the asuras:
“The gods are indeed victorious.
What if we were to engage in battle with the gods a second time?
And a second time, monks, the asuras engaged in battle with the gods.
A second time, monks, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
Having been defeated, monks, the asuras fled toward the south, while the devas pursued them.
Then, monks, it occurred to the asuras:
"The gods are indeed victorious.
What if we were to engage in battle with the gods for a third time?
And for a third time, monks, the asuras engaged in battle with the gods.
A third time, monks, the devas were victorious and the asuras were defeated.
Having been defeated, monks, the frightened asuras entered the city of the asuras.
And once they had reached the city of the asuras, monks, this thought occurred to them:
‘Now we dwell with ourselves having gone to the safety from fear; we are no longer subject to being acted upon by the devas.
And it occurred to the devas too, monks:
‘Now the asuras dwell with themselves having gone to the safety from fear; they are no longer subject to being acted upon by us.’

In the same way, monks, at whatever time a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion—at that time, monks, it occurs to the monk:
"I now dwell having gone to a place of safety from fear; I am no longer subject to Māra."
“Bhikkhus, even to Māra the Evil One it occurs thus:
‘The bhikkhu now dwells having entered upon a refuge from fear; he is no longer to be dealt with by me.
Bhikkhus, at whatever time a bhikkhu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna…”
When he enters and dwells in the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna,
at that time, bhikkhus, it occurs to the bhikkhu thus:
‘I now dwell having gone to the safety from fear; I am no longer subject to Māra.
Monks, it occurs to Māra the Evil One as well:
‘The monk now dwells having gone to the safety from fear; he is no longer subject to me.’

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of the infinity of space—at that time, bhikkhus, it is said of that bhikkhu:
‘He has made an end of Māra; having struck down Māra’s eye, he has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One; he has crossed over attachment to the world.’”

“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness … by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness,
thinking ‘there is nothing,’ enters and dwells in the base of nothingness … by completely transcending the base of nothingness,
enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception …”

“By completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.

This, monks, is called a monk who has made an end of Māra, who, having struck down Māra’s eye so that it is footless, has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One, and has crossed over attachment to the world.
Thus was the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.40 4. Mahāvagga Nāgasutta (The Elephant) “Monks, there are these four kinds of elephants. What four? The elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, yet is not trained; the elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, and is also well-trained; the elephant that is not well-bred, not of noble lineage, not born of a good family, yet is well-trained; and the elephant that is neither well-bred nor of noble lineage nor born of a good family, nor is it well-trained. These, monks, are the four kinds of elephants. In the same way, monks, there are these four kinds of persons similar to elephants. What four?

The person who is like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, yet is not trained; the person who is like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, and is also well-trained; the person who is like an elephant that is not well-bred, not of noble lineage, not born of a good family, yet is well-trained; and the person who is like an elephant that is neither well-bred nor of noble lineage nor born of a good family, nor is it well-trained. And how, monks, is a person like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, yet is not trained? Here, monks, someone is of noble birth—whether a khattiya by birth, a brahmin by birth, or a householder by birth—and he possesses great wealth, abundant property, and vast possessions. He has much gold and bullion stored away, much silver and bullion stored away, many fields and lands, many buildings and dwellings, many wives and concubines, many male and female slaves, and many workers and servants. Yet he does not give gifts, does not perform meritorious deeds, and does not establish an offering for travelers. This, monks, is called a person like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, yet is not trained. And how, monks, is a person like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, and is also well-trained? Here, monks, someone is of noble birth—whether a khattiya by birth, a brahmin by birth, or a householder by birth—and he possesses great wealth, abundant property, and vast possessions. He has much gold and bullion stored away, much silver and bullion stored away, many fields and lands, many buildings and dwellings, many wives and concubines, many male and female slaves, and many workers and servants. And he gives gifts, performs meritorious deeds, and establishes an offering for travelers. This, monks, is called a person like an elephant that is well-bred, of noble lineage, born of a good family, and is also well-trained. And how, monks, is a person like an elephant that is not well-bred, not of noble lineage, not born of a good family, yet is well-trained? Here, monks, someone is of low birth—whether a candala by birth, a veṇa by birth, a nesada by birth, a rathakāra by birth, or a pukkusa by birth—and he possesses little wealth, meager property, and scant possessions. He has little gold and bullion stored away, little silver and bullion stored away, few fields and lands, few buildings and dwellings, few wives and concubines, few male and female slaves, and few workers and servants. Yet he gives gifts, performs meritorious deeds, and establishes an offering for travelers. This, monks, is called a person like an elephant that is not well-bred, not of noble lineage, not born of a good family, yet is well-trained. And how, monks, is a person like an elephant that is neither well-bred nor of noble lineage nor born of a good family, nor is it well-trained? Here, monks, someone is of low birth—whether a candala by birth, a veṇa by birth, a nesada by birth, a rathakāra by birth, or a pukkusa by birth—and he possesses little wealth, meager property, and scant possessions. He has little gold and bullion stored away, little silver and bullion stored away, few fields and lands, few buildings and dwellings, few wives and concubines, few male and female slaves, and few workers and servants. And he does not give gifts, does not perform meritorious deeds, and does not establish an offering for travelers. This, monks, is called a person like an elephant that is neither well-bred nor of noble lineage nor born of a good family, nor is it well-trained. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons similar to elephants.”
“Bhikkhus, on whatever occasion a forest-dwelling elephant, intent on his feeding ground, has elephants, female elephants, elephant calves,
and elephant cubs going ahead of him and cutting off the tips of the grasses— by that, bhikkhus, [he is not disturbed].”
The forest-dwelling elephant is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted. Monks,
on whatever occasion the elephants, the female elephants, the young male elephants,
and the baby elephants eat the broken-off branches while the forest-dwelling elephant is intent upon his feeding ground, by that, monks—
The forest-dwelling elephant is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted. Monks,

at whatever time the elephants, the female elephants, the young elephants, and the calf-elephants go ahead of the forest-dwelling elephant who has entered the bathing pool and churn the water with their trunks, because of that—
“Monks, the forest elephant is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.

Monks, at whatever time the female elephants go along rubbing their bodies against that of the forest elephant who has emerged from his bathing place, on that occasion, monks, the forest elephant is distressed, ashamed, and disgusted.
At that time, monks, it occurs to the forest elephant thus:”
‘At present, I live crowded with male elephants, female elephants, calf-elephants, and baby elephants.
I eat grass with its tips broken off, and they eat my broken-off branches; I drink turbid water, and when I emerge from the bathing pool, female elephants come rubbing their bodies against mine.
What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the herd?’
Then, at a later time, one [elephant] lived secluded from the herd; it ate only grass with uncut tips, and they did not eat its broken-off branches;
it drank only clear water, and when it emerged from the bathing pool, the female elephants did not go along rubbing their bodies against it.
At that time, monks, it occurs to the forest-dwelling elephant:
"Formerly, I lived crowded among male elephants, female elephants, elephant calves, and elephant cubs;
I ate grass with its tips broken off, and they ate my broken-off branches until they were scattered, and the waters [were turbid]."
I drank the waters, and when I had emerged from the bathing place, female elephants approached, rubbing their bodies against my body.
But now I dwell alone, secluded from the crowd; I eat grass with uncut tips, they do not eat from my broken-off branches, I drink undisturbed waters, and [emerge] from the bathing place.
"And when I have emerged, let no female elephants come walking along, rubbing their bodies against mine.
Having thus broken off a branch with his trunk and rubbed his body with that branch, he, being satisfied, withdraws his trunk.
In the same way, monks, at whatever time a monk dwells crowded among monks and nuns...
When there are laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and disciples of other sects [approaching him],
at that time, monks, it occurs to a bhikkhu: “At present,
I am dwelling crowded by bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, and disciples of other sects.”
‘What if I were to dwell alone, withdrawn from the crowd?
He frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within, and he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from indecision regarding wholesome states, and he purifies his mind of doubt.
Having thus abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—

Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
Being satisfied, he withdraws his trunk.
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought... [he enters] the second jhāna...
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
Being satisfied, he withdraws his trunk.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
Being satisfied, he withdraws his trunk.
With the complete surmounting of the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
By completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking “there is nothing,” he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness...
by completely transcending the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...

by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
Thus, being well-pleased, he withdraws his trunk.
Thus ends the ninth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.41
4. Mahāvagga:
The Discourse to Tapussa (AN 9.41, PTS AN iv 438)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Mallas at a town of the Mallas named Uruvelakappa.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Uruvelakappa for alms.
Having walked for alms in Uruvelakappa, after his meal, on his return from the alms round, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Stay right here, Ānanda, until I have entered the Great Wood for my midday rest.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, having entered the Great Wood, sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then the householder Tapussa approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached and paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Tapussa said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable Ānanda, we are householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, rejoicing in sensual pleasures, and finding happiness in sensual pleasures."

"Venerable sir, for us householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, who delight in sensual pleasures, who rejoice in sensual pleasures, and who are intoxicated by sensual pleasures, this renunciation appears like a precipice.

But I have heard this, venerable sir: 'In this Dhamma and Discipline, the minds of many young bhikkhus leap forward at renunciation, find confidence in it, settle upon it, and are liberated in it, seeing it as peace.
Yet, venerable sir, in this Dhamma and Discipline, renunciation is something foreign to many people, namely these bhikkhus."
“Householder, this is a topic worthy of being brought before the Blessed One for an audience.
Come, householder, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached him, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
We will bear it in mind exactly as the Blessed One explains it.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Tapussa replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda went together with the householder Tapussa to where the Blessed One was.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this householder Tapussa says:
‘Venerable Ānanda, we are householders who enjoy sensual pleasures, delighting in sensual pleasures, rejoicing in sensual pleasures, and exulting in sensual pleasures.
For us, venerable sir, householders who enjoy, delight in, rejoice in, and exult in sensual pleasures, there is a precipice.’”
“It appears as if it were so, namely, renunciation.
“I have heard this, Bhante: ‘In this Dhamma and Discipline, the minds of many young bhikkhus leap forward, find confidence, become settled, and are liberated in renunciation, seeing it as peace.
Yet, Bhante, in this Dhamma and Discipline, renunciation is something that many people find disagreeable for the bhikkhus.”
“So it is, Ānanda; so it is, Ānanda.
Even before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta and not yet fully enlightened, this occurred to me:
‘Excellent is renunciation! Excellent is seclusion!’”
“Ānanda, my mind did not leap up at renunciation, nor did it become confident, settled, or liberated, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘What is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap up at renunciation, nor become confident, settled, or liberated, even though I see it as peaceful?’”
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
“I have not seen the danger in sensual pleasures, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not realized the benefit in renunciation, nor have I pursued it.
Therefore, my mind does not leap forward toward renunciation, does not find confidence in it, does not settle in it, and is not liberated in it, even though I see it as peaceful.”
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me: "If,
having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, and having attained the benefit in renunciation, were to dwell in it,
it is possible that my mind would leap forward into renunciation, become confident, become settled, and be liberated, seeing it as peace."
Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, I cultivated that [insight] frequently; having realized the benefit in renunciation, I pursued it.
My mind, Ānanda, leaped forward into renunciation, became confident, settled, and was liberated, seeing it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
While I was dwelling in this state of abiding, Ānanda, perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire occurred to me. That was a source of affliction for me.
Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise in one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, when perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire occurred to me, that was a source of affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
“What if, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, I were to enter and dwell in the second jhāna?
But, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into that state of non-applied thought; it did not settle, become established, or find release, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

"What now is the cause, what is the condition, because of which my mind does not leap forward into the state without directed thought, does not become placid, does not settle, and is not liberated, even though I see it as peace?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘I have not seen the danger in applied thoughts, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not attained the benefit in the absence of applied thoughts, nor have I pursued it.
Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the state without applied thought; it does not find confidence, does not settle, and is not liberated, even though I see this as peace.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘If, having seen the danger in applied thoughts, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, and having attained the benefit in non-applied thought,
I were to pursue it, it is possible that my mind would leap forward into non-applied thought,
become confident, become settled, and be liberated, seeing this as peace.’
Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in applied thoughts, I cultivated that [insight] frequently; and having realized the benefit in the absence of applied thought, I pursued it.
My mind, Ānanda, leaped forward into the state without applied thought, became serene, settled, and was liberated, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought... I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna.
While I was dwelling in this abiding, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by applied thought occurred to me. That was an affliction for me.

Just as, Ānanda, pain might arise for one who is happy only to the extent that it is an affliction, even so, when perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by applied thought occurred to me, that was an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to me:

"What if, with the fading away of rapture, I were to dwell in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experience happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous'—thus entering the third jhāna?"
‘...and having attained it, may I dwell therein.
Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward the state free from rapture, nor did it find confidence, settle, or become liberated, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

“What now is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap up at the state free from rapture, does not find confidence, does not become settled, and is not liberated in it, even though I see this as peace?
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to me:
“I have not seen the danger in rapture, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not attained the benefit in the state free from rapture, nor have I pursued it.”
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward, does not settle, does not become established, and is not liberated in the state free from rapture, even though I see it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in rapture, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, and having attained the benefit in the state free from rapture..."
"I would cultivate that state; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward, gain confidence, become settled, and be liberated in the absence of rapture, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in rapture, I cultivated that [absence of rapture] frequently, and having attained the benefit in the absence of rapture, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leapt forward, became serene, settled, and was liberated in the state free from rapture, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, I dwelt having attained the third jhāna...
While I was dwelling in this abiding, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by rapture still occurred to me; that was a source of affliction for me.”
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise in one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, these perceptions and mental engagements accompanied by rapture occurred to me. That was indeed an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:"

‘What if, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I were to enter and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity?
However, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward that state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, nor did it find confidence, settle, or become liberated, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

“What now could be the cause, what the condition, why my mind does not leap up at neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, does not settle down in it, does not find stability in it, and is not liberated in it, even though I see this as peace?
Then, Ānanda, it occurred to me:
“I have not seen the danger in the pleasure of equanimity, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not attained the benefit in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, nor have I pursued it.”
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward toward the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state; it does not settle, become steady, or find liberation in it, even though I see it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in the pleasure of equanimity, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, then the benefit in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state would [become apparent]."

"Having attained that, I cultivated it; and it was possible for my mind to leap forward into, to find confidence in, to settle in, and to be liberated in that state which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, seeing it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the pleasure of equanimity, I cultivated that [state] frequently; and having attained the benefit in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant state, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leapt forward, became serene, settled, and was liberated in the state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure... I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna.
While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and mental explorations accompanied by equanimity occurred to me; that became a source of affliction for me.”
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, these perceptions and mental engagements associated with equanimity occurred to me. That was indeed an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:"

‘What if, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, perceiving “space is infinite,” I were to enter and dwell in the base of infinite space?
But, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward the base of infinite space, nor did it find confidence, settle, or become liberated in it, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

‘What now is the cause, what is the condition, why my mind does not leap forward into the base of infinite space, does not find confidence in it, does not settle down in it, and is not released into it, even though I see it as peace?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘I have not seen the danger in forms, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not attained the benefit in the base of infinite space, nor have I pursued it.’
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the base of infinite space, does not become confident in it, does not settle in it, and is not liberated in it, because I do not see it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in forms, I were to cultivate that repeatedly, and [see] the benefit in the base of infinite space..."
"Having attained that, I would cultivate it; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward, gain confidence, become settled, and be liberated in the base of infinite space, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in forms, I cultivated that [insight] frequently; having attained the benefit in the base of infinite space, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leapt into, settled in, remained fixed upon, and was liberated in the base of infinite space, seeing it as peace.

Having completely transcended perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite space.
While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements associated with form occurred to me; that was a source of affliction for me.”
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, when perceptions and mental attentions associated with form occurred to me, that was an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, were to enter and dwell in the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving]: "Consciousness is infinite"?
Yet, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward into the base of infinite consciousness; it did not find confidence, it did not settle, and it was not liberated, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

"What now is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward into the base of infinite consciousness, does not become confident, does not settle, and is not liberated in it, even though I see it as peaceful?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"I have not seen the danger in the base of infinite space and have not cultivated that; I have not attained the benefit in the base of infinite consciousness and have not pursued it."
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward toward the base of infinite consciousness, nor does it find confidence, settle, or become liberated in it, as I see this [base] as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in the base of infinite space, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, then [the mind would not leap forward] in the base of infinite consciousness..."

"Having realized its benefit, I would cultivate it; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward into the base of infinite consciousness, become confident in it, settle in it, and be liberated in it, seeing it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the base of infinite space, I cultivated that [insight], and having realized the benefit in the base of infinite consciousness, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leaped forward into the base of infinite consciousness, became serene, settled, and was liberated in it, seeing it as peace.
Having completely transcended the base of infinite space, Ānanda, I entered and dwelt in the base of infinite consciousness, [perceiving]: ‘Consciousness is infinite.
While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space still occurred to me. That was a source of affliction for me.”
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, these perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite space occurred to me. That was an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving “there is nothing,” were to enter and dwell in the base of nothingness?
But, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward the base of nothingness, nor did it find confidence, nor did it become settled, nor was it liberated, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘What now is the cause, what is the reason, why my mind does not leap forward into the base of nothingness, does not become placid, firm, and liberated, even though I see it as peace?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
‘I have not seen the danger in the base of infinite consciousness, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not attained the benefit of the base of nothingness, nor have I pursued it.’
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the dimension of nothingness; it does not find confidence, settle, or become liberated in it, as I do not see it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in the dimension of infinite consciousness, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, then [the mind would settle] in the dimension of nothingness..."

“Having realized its benefit, I would cultivate it; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward into the base of nothingness, become confident in it, remain settled in it, and be liberated in it, seeing it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the base of infinite consciousness, I cultivated that [insight], and having realized the benefit in the base of nothingness, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leapt forward into the base of nothingness, became serene, settled, and was liberated in it, seeing it as peace.
Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking ‘there is nothing,’ I entered and dwelt in the base of nothingness.
While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of infinite consciousness still occurred to me; that was a source of affliction for me.”
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, consciousness-sphere-accompanied perceptions and mental engagements were occurring to me. That was an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:"
‘What if I, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, were to enter and dwell in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
But, Ānanda, my mind did not leap toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor did it find confidence, settle, or become liberated in it, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

"What now could be the cause, what the condition, why my mind does not leap forward into the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, does not find confidence in it, does not settle down in it, and is not liberated in it, even though I see it as peace?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

"I have not seen the danger in the dimension of nothingness, nor have I cultivated that; I have not attained the benefit in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor have I pursued it."

"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor does it find confidence in it, nor does it settle in it, nor is it liberated in it, even though I see it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:
"If, having seen the danger in the base of nothingness, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, [then my mind would leap forward into the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception...]"

"Having realized its benefit, I would cultivate it; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward, gain confidence, become settled, and be liberated in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, seeing it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, at a later time, having seen the danger in the base of nothingness, I cultivated that [insight], and having realized the benefit in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I cultivated it.
"Ānanda, my mind leapt forward into the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; it became placid, settled, and liberated, seeing it as peace.
Thus, Ānanda, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, I entered and dwelt in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
While I was dwelling in this state, Ānanda, perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of nothingness still occurred to me, and that was a source of affliction for me."
"Just as, Ānanda, if suffering were to arise for one who is happy, it would lead only to affliction;
even so, when perceptions and mental engagements associated with the base of nothingness occurred to me, that became an affliction for me.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, were to enter and dwell in the cessation of perception and feeling?
However, Ānanda, my mind did not leap forward toward the cessation of perception and feeling, nor did it find confidence, settle, or become liberated in it, even though I saw it as peaceful.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to me:

“What now could be the cause, what the reason, why my mind does not leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, does not find confidence in it, does not become settled in it, and is not liberated in it, even though I see it as peaceful?
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

“I have not seen the danger in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, nor have I cultivated that [insight]; I have not realized the benefit in the cessation of perception and feeling, nor have I pursued it.”
"Therefore, my mind does not leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, nor does it find confidence in it, settle in it, or become liberated in it, because I do not see it as peace.
Then, Ānanda, this occurred to me:

"If, having seen the danger in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I were to cultivate that [insight] frequently, then [the mind would leap forward into] the cessation of perception and feeling..."

“Having realized its benefit, I would cultivate it; for it is possible that my mind might leap forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, become settled, established, and liberated in it, seeing it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, after some time, having seen the danger in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I cultivated that [insight]; and having realized the benefit in the cessation of perception and feeling, I cultivated it.
“Ānanda, my mind leapt forward into the cessation of perception and feeling, it became settled, stayed, and was liberated in it as I saw it as peace.

Then, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I entered and dwelt in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, the taints went to their destruction in me.
And for as long as I had not yet mastered these nine successive attainments of dwelling in this way, both forward and backward...”

I entered them and emerged from them; yet, Ānanda, I did not then declare in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, that I had awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
But when, Ānanda, I had thus [mastered] these nine successive dwellings in attainment in forward and reverse order...

I entered them and emerged from them; then, Ānanda, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And knowledge and vision arose in me:
“Unshakable is my liberation of mind; this is my final birth; now there is no further becoming. Tenth.

5. The Chapter on Asceticism: The Discourse on Confined Space (Sāmaññavagga Sambādhasutta) “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who lives in a confined space, not for one who lives in an open space. And how, bhikkhus, does one live in a confined space? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, without developing the mind’s liberation through the cessation of sensual lust; he dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, without developing the mind’s liberation through the cessation of ill will; he dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, without developing the mind’s liberation through the cessation of sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, without developing the mind’s liberation through the cessation of restlessness and remorse; he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, without developing the mind’s liberation through the cessation of doubt. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He does not understand as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one lives in a confined space. This Dhamma is for one who lives in a confined space, not for one who lives in an open space. And how, bhikkhus, does one live in an open space? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind unobsessed by sensual lust, having developed the mind’s liberation through the cessation of sensual lust; he dwells with a mind unobsessed by ill will, having developed the mind’s liberation through the cessation of ill will; he dwells with a mind unobsessed by sloth and torpor, having developed the mind’s liberation through the cessation of sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind unobsessed by restlessness and remorse, having developed the mind’s liberation through the cessation of restlessness and remorse; he dwells with a mind unobsessed by doubt, having developed the mind’s liberation through the cessation of doubt. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. It is in such a way, bhikkhus, that one lives in an open space. This Dhamma is for one who lives in an open space, not for one who lives in a confined space.”
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park.
Then the Venerable Udāyī approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend, this was said by the divine son Pañcālacaṇḍa:
‘The narrow space has been traversed by the one of vast intelligence who does not know [the way].’”
“The Buddha, the Sage, the Bull among men who has withdrawn [from the world], has awakened to jhāna.
“Friend, what is the confinement, and what is said by the Blessed One to be the attainment of space within that confinement?”
“Friends, these five cords of sensual pleasure have been called confinement by the Blessed One.
Which five?

Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tactile objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.]”
Sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … [and so on] …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, friends, are the five cords of sensual pleasure which the Blessed One has called confinement.
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
"To this extent, friend, the Blessed One has spoken of attaining space within confinement by way of a method.
Yet, even there, there is still confinement.
And what is the confinement there?"
In this case, whatever applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have not yet ceased—this is the confinement here.
Furthermore, friends, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna.
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of open space within confinement by way of a figurative method (*pariyāya*).
In that case, there is a constriction. And what is the constriction there?
That very joy which has not yet ceased—this is the constriction here.
Furthermore, friends, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in the third jhāna...
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of open space within confinement by way of a figurative expression;
yet there is still confinement therein.
And what, in this case, is the constriction?
That very pleasure of equanimity which has not yet ceased—this is the constriction here.
Furthermore, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure... [and so on]... a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
"To this extent, friend, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of space within confinement by way of a figurative expression.
Yet, there is still confinement therein. And what is the confinement there?"
In this case, whatever perception of form has not yet ceased—that is the confinement here.

Furthermore, friends, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, [perceiving] "space is infinite.
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of open space within confinement by way of a figurative expression.
In that case, there is a confinement.
And what is the confinement therein?
That the perception of the base of infinite space has not yet ceased—this is the confinement here.
Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of open space within confinement, in a figurative sense.
Yet, in that case, there is still confinement.
And what, in this case, is the confinement?
That the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has not yet ceased—this is the confinement here.
Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
"To this extent, friend, the Blessed One has spoken of attaining space within confinement by way of a gradual method.
Yet, in that regard, there is still confinement. And what is the confinement there?"
In this case, that the perception of the base of nothingness has not yet ceased is the confinement here.
Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of space within confinement by way of a gradual method.
In that regard, there is a constriction.
And what is the constriction therein?
That the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has not yet ceased—this is the constriction here.

"Furthermore, friends, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
To this extent, friends, the Blessed One has spoken of the attainment of space within confinement in the non-figurative sense. Thus was the first [discourse].
