The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga) The Discourse on the Body-Witness (Kāyasakkhīsutta) “Monks, there is one person who is a body-witness. What kind of person is a body-witness? Here, monks, a monk has experienced for himself with direct knowledge those peaceful liberations that transcend forms, which are formless, and having entered upon them, remains therein. Yet he does not attain final Nibbāna in this very life; rather, he attains final Nibbāna upon the dissolution of the body. This is called a person who is a body-witness. This, monks, is the first kind of person.”
“Friend, it is said, ‘a body-witness, a body-witness.
To what extent, friend, is one called a body-witness by the Blessed One?”
"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
And in whatever way that sphere [of the first jhāna] exists, in that very way he dwells having touched it with the body.
To this extent, friends, one is called a 'body-witness' by the Blessed One in a figurative sense."
Furthermore, friends, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna.
In whatever way that sphere [of experience] exists, in that very way he dwells having touched it with his body.
To this extent, friend, one is called a "body-witness" by the Blessed One in a figurative sense.

Furthermore, friend, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking "space is infinite," a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
In whatever way that base is, in that very way he dwells having touched it with his body.
It is in this way, friend, that one is called a "body-witness" by the Blessed One in a figurative sense...

Furthermore, friend, a bhikkhu, having completely transcended the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
"In whatever way that sphere [of experience] exists, in that very way he dwells having touched it with the body.
To this extent, friend, one is called a 'body-witness' by the Blessed One in the direct sense.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.44 5. Sāmaññavagga Paññāvimuttasutta (The Discourse on Liberation through Wisdom) “Monks, there are these nine persons found existing in the world. What nine? The person liberated by wisdom, the person liberated both ways, the body-witness, the one attained to view, the one liberated by faith, the Dhamma-follower, the faith-follower, the one who has entered the stream, and the ordinary worldling. And what, monks, is the person liberated by wisdom? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; yet he does not possess the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a person liberated by wisdom. And what, monks, is the person liberated both ways? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering;

and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This is called a person liberated both ways. And what, monks, is the body-witness? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, yet he does not dwell having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide. This is called a body-witness. And what, monks, is the one attained to view? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, and he dwells having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide, yet he does not dwell having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice. This is called one attained to view. And what, monks, is the one liberated by faith? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, and he dwells having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide, and he has fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, yet he does not dwell having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice. This is called one liberated by faith. And what, monks, is the Dhamma-follower? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, and he dwells having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide, and he has fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, and he dwells having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, yet he does not dwell having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice. This is called a Dhamma-follower. And what, monks, is the faith-follower? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, and he dwells having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide, and he has fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, and he dwells having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, yet he does not dwell having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice. This is called a faith-follower. And what, monks, is the one who has entered the stream? Here, monks, a certain person possesses wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; and he also possesses the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering, and he dwells having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide, and he has fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, and he dwells having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, and he dwells having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice, yet he does not dwell having fully understood and mastered them through repeated practice. This is called one who has entered the stream. And what, monks, is the ordinary worldling? Here, monks, a certain person does not possess wisdom that is noble, penetrating, leading to the complete destruction of suffering; nor does he possess the noble concentration that is accompanied by the higher mind and leads to the complete destruction of suffering; nor does he dwell having realized with his own direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for which those noble ones enter and abide. This is called an ordinary worldling.”
“Friend, it is said: ‘One liberated by wisdom, one liberated by wisdom.
To what extent, friend, has one been called ‘liberated by wisdom’ by the Blessed One?”
“Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures … enters and dwells in the first jhāna;
and he understands this with wisdom.
To this extent too, friends, one is said by the Blessed One to be ‘liberated by wisdom’ in a figurative sense …” [and so on].

"Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
It is to this extent, friends, that one is called 'liberated by wisdom' by the Blessed One in the direct sense."
Third.

The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga) The Discourse on Final Nibbāna (Parinibbānasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these nine grounds for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. What nine? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of lust for sensual pleasures; he has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising.

This is the first ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (2) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of lust for the body; he has abandoned lust for the body, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the second ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (3) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of lust for form; he has abandoned lust for form, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the third ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (4) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of lust for existence; he has abandoned lust for existence, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the fourth ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (5) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of hatred; he has abandoned hatred, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the fifth ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (6) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of delusion; he has abandoned delusion, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the sixth ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (7) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of agitation; he has abandoned agitation, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the seventh ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (8) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of conceit; he has abandoned conceit, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the eighth ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. (9) Again, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind devoid of ignorance; he has abandoned ignorance, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, obliterated it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. This is the ninth ground for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now. These, bhikkhus, are the nine grounds for the attainment of final Nibbāna here and now.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.52 6. Khemavagga Khemasutta (The Discourse on Safety) “Bhikkhus, there are these nine grounds for the origination of non-fear. What nine? ‘This one is a murderer,’ bhikkhus, this is the first ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one is a thief,’ this is the second ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one is an adulterer,’ this is the third ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one speaks falsehood,’ this is the fourth ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one speaks divisively,’ this is the fifth ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one speaks harshly,’ this is the sixth ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one speaks idle chatter,’ this is the seventh ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one is covetous,’ this is the eighth ground for the origination of non-fear. ‘This one harbors ill will,’ this is the ninth ground for the origination of non-fear. These, bhikkhus, are the nine grounds for the origination of non-fear. But there are, bhikkhus, these nine grounds for the origination of fear. What nine? ‘This one is a murderer,’ bhikkhus, this is the first ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one is a thief,’ this is the second ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one is an adulterer,’ this is the third ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one speaks falsehood,’ this is the fourth ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one speaks divisively,’ this is the fifth ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one speaks harshly,’ this is the sixth ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one speaks idle chatter,’ this is the seventh ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one is covetous,’ this is the eighth ground for the origination of fear. ‘This one harbors ill will,’ this is the ninth ground for the origination of fear. These, bhikkhus, are the nine grounds for the origination of fear. But there are, bhikkhus, these nine grounds for the origination of safety. What nine? ‘This one is not a murderer,’ bhikkhus, this is the first ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one is not a thief,’ this is the second ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one is not an adulterer,’ this is the third ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one does not speak falsehood,’ this is the fourth ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one does not speak divisively,’ this is the fifth ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one does not speak harshly,’ this is the sixth ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one does not speak idle chatter,’ this is the seventh ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one is not covetous,’ this is the eighth ground for the origination of safety. ‘This one is not one who harbors ill will,’ this is the ninth ground for the origination of safety. These, bhikkhus, are the nine grounds for the origination of safety.”

And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who has turned away from the deathless? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who holds wrong view, who holds wrong intention, who holds wrong speech, who holds wrong action, who holds wrong livelihood, who holds wrong effort, who holds wrong mindfulness, and who holds wrong concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who has turned away from the deathless. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is heading toward the deathless? 6. Khemavagga Passaddhisutta (AN 9.58, PTS AN iv 455) “Monks, there are these five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These, monks, are the five hindrances. Furthermore, monks, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of volitional formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. These, monks, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Now, monks, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding these five hindrances and these five aggregates subject to clinging? The gratification in the case of the five hindrances and the five aggregates subject to clinging is simply the pleasure and joy that arise from them. The danger in the case of the five hindrances and the five aggregates subject to clinging is that they are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. The escape from the five hindrances and the five aggregates subject to clinging is the complete dispassion toward them, their fading away, and their cessation. When a monk understands as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five hindrances and these five aggregates subject to clinging, he is called a monk who has seen the Dhamma, one who lives having reached the Dhamma, a noble disciple who has arrived at the right Dhamma, who has transcended the plane of ordinary people, and who has entered the plane of the noble ones.”

Khemavagga Anupubbapassaddhisutta (AN 9.59) “Bhikkhus, when these five factors are developed and cultivated, they lead to gradual serenity, gradual tranquility, and gradual leading to the deathless. Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu generates desire to arouse energy; he exerts his mind and strives. He dwells contemplating impermanence in all formations, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called, bhikkhus, developing the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu develop the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu arouses energy, not casting off the duty of cultivating wholesome qualities; he dwells contemplating impermanence in all formations, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called, bhikkhus, developing the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu develop the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving? This is called, bhikkhus, developing the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu develop the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu investigates, examines, and scrutinizes those very phenomena with wisdom; he dwells contemplating impermanence in all formations, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment. This is called, bhikkhus, developing the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. When, bhikkhus, these five factors are developed and cultivated in this way, they lead to gradual serenity, gradual tranquility, and gradual leading to the deathless.”

Why is that? Because, monks, when lust arises in a person, it leads to his own affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both. It brings about vexation, grief, and despair. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not tolerate lust when it arises. [The Blessed One said: “Monks, when hatred arises in a person… When delusion arises in a person… When anger arises in a person… When hostility arises in a person… When denigration arises in a person… When insolence arises in a person… When envy arises in a person… When miserliness arises in a person… When deceitfulness arises in a person… When craftiness arises in a person… When obstinacy arises in a person… When arrogance arises in a person… When conceit arises in a person… When vanity arises in a person… When negligence arises in a person, it is not for his welfare, nor for his happiness, nor for the benefit of many people, nor for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans.

Why is that? Because, monks, when negligence arises in a person, it leads to his own affliction, to the affliction of others, and to the affliction of both. It brings about vexation, grief, and despair. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall not tolerate negligence when it arises. [The Blessed One said: “Monks, when lust has not arisen in a person, it is for his welfare, for his happiness, for the benefit of many people, and for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans. Why is that? Because, monks, when lust has not arisen in a person, it does not lead to his own affliction, nor to the affliction of others, nor to the affliction of both. It does not bring about vexation, grief, and despair. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘When lust has not arisen, we shall strive to prevent its arising; and when it has arisen, we shall strive to abandon it. [The Blessed One said: “Monks, when hatred has not arisen in a person… When delusion has not arisen in a person… When anger has not arisen in a person… When hostility has not arisen in a person… When denigration has not arisen in a person… When insolence has not arisen in a person… When envy has not arisen in a person… When miserliness has not arisen in a person… When deceitfulness has not arisen in a person… When craftiness has not arisen in a person… When obstinacy has not arisen in a person… When arrogance has not arisen in a person… When conceit has not arisen in a person… When vanity has not arisen in a person… When negligence has not arisen in a person, it is for his welfare, for his happiness, for the benefit of many people, and for the welfare and happiness of gods and humans. [The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these five lower fetters. What five? They are: self-identity view, doubt, attachment to rules and observances, sensual lust, and ill will.
